<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>You will be given a problem followed by an enumerated list of 11 candidate solutions. Your task is to systematically analyze these solutions to identify the best approach.

Problem: Given matrix $\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ and vector $\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$, solve the following optimization problem:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\underset{\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\text{minimize}} & \boldsymbol{\beta}^T \mathbf{M} \, \boldsymbol{\beta}\\
\text{subject to} & \boldsymbol{\mu}^T \boldsymbol{\beta} \geq \sigma\\
& \boldsymbol{1}^T \boldsymbol{\beta} \leq 1\\
& \beta_i \geq 0, \quad \forall i \in \{ 1,\, 2,\, \dots, \, p\}
\end{array}
\]
where $\boldsymbol{1} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ is a vector of ones.

Solutions:
Solution 0:
**Solution (KKT‑analysis).**  

Put  

\[
C=\Bigl\{\beta\in\mathbb {R}^{p}\;{\Big|}\;
\mu ^{T}\beta \ge \sigma ,\;
\mathbf 1^{T}\beta \le 1 ,\;
\beta \ge 0\Bigr\}.
\]

The objective \(f(\beta)=\beta ^{T}M\beta\) is convex when \(M\) is symmetric
positive‑semidefinite, hence the problem is a convex quadratic programme.
Introduce Lagrange multipliers  

\[
\lambda \ge 0\quad (\mu ^{T}\beta \ge \sigma ),\qquad
\nu   \ge 0\quad (\mathbf 1^{T}\beta \le 1),\qquad
\alpha   =(\alpha _1,\dots ,\alpha _p)^{T},\;\alpha_i\ge 0
\;(\beta_i\ge 0).
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta ,\lambda ,\nu ,\alpha )
      =\beta ^{T}M\beta
        +\lambda (\sigma-\mu ^{T}\beta )
        +\nu (\mathbf 1^{T}\beta -1)
        -\alpha ^{T}\beta .
\]

---

### 1.  KKT conditions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{(stationarity)}   &&\nabla_\beta\mathcal L
   = 2M\beta-\lambda \mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\alpha =0,\\[2mm]
&\text{(primal feasibility)} &&\beta\in C,\\[2mm]
&\text{(dual feasibility)}   &&\lambda \ge 0,\ \nu\ge 0,\ \alpha\ge 0,\\[2mm]
&\text{(complementary slackness)} &&
   \lambda(\sigma-\mu ^{T}\beta )=0,\;
   \nu(\mathbf 1^{T}\beta-1)=0,\;
   \alpha_i\beta_i =0,\;i=1,\dots ,p .
\end{aligned}
\tag{KKT}
\]

---

### 2.  Solving the stationarity condition  

If a component \(\beta_i>0\) then, by complementary slackness,
\(\alpha_i=0\).  Let  

\[
A=\{i\mid \beta_i>0\},\qquad
\bar A=\{i\mid \beta_i=0\}.
\]

For the active indices we have  

\[
2M_{A A}\beta_A-\lambda\mu_A+\nu\mathbf 1_A=0,
\tag{1}
\]

where the subscript \(A\) denotes the restriction of a matrix or vector
to the rows/columns indexed by \(A\).  Equation (1) gives  

\[
\beta_A
   =\frac{1}{2}\,M_{A A}^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu_A-\nu\mathbf 1_A\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

For the inactive indices (\(i\in\bar A\)) the stationarity condition reads  

\[
\alpha_i =-\bigl[2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1\bigr]_i \ge 0 .
\tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Determination of the multipliers  

Two linear constraints can be either active (\(=\) ) or inactive (\(<\) ).
Accordingly we have four possibilities.

---

#### (a)  Both constraints inactive  

\(\lambda =\nu =0\) and (2) gives \(\beta=0\).  
This is feasible only when \(\sigma\le0\); otherwise it is discarded.

---

#### (b)  Only \(\mu ^{T}\beta\ge\sigma\) active  

\(\lambda>0,\;\nu =0\).  From (2)

\[
\beta =\frac{\lambda}{2}\,M^{-1}\mu .
\]

The multiplier is obtained from the active constraint  

\[
\mu ^{T}\beta =\sigma \Longrightarrow
\lambda =\frac{2\sigma}{\mu ^{T}M^{-1}\mu } .
\]

The candidate is admissible if  

\[
\mathbf 1^{T}\beta\le 1,\qquad \beta\ge 0 .
\tag{4}
\]

If (4) holds, this \(\beta\) is optimal.

---

#### (c)  Only \(\mathbf 1^{T}\beta\le1\) active  

\(\lambda =0,\;\nu>0\).  From (2)

\[
\beta =-\frac{\nu}{2}\,M^{-1}\mathbf 1 .
\]

Because \(\beta\ge0\) we need \(M^{-1}\mathbf 1\le 0\) component‑wise.
The multiplier follows from the active constraint  

\[
\mathbf 1^{T}\beta =1\Longrightarrow
\nu =\frac{2}{\mathbf 1^{T}M^{-1}\mathbf 1 } .
\]

If the resulting \(\beta\) also satisfies \(\mu ^{T}\beta\ge\sigma\) it is optimal.

---

#### (d)  Both linear constraints active  

\(\lambda>0,\;\nu>0\).  
Put  

\[
a=\mu ^{T}M^{-1}\mu ,\qquad
b=\mu ^{T}M^{-1}\mathbf 1 ,\qquad
c=\mathbf 1^{T}M^{-1}\mathbf 1 ,
\qquad \Delta =ac-b^{2}>0 .
\]

From (2) and the two active constraints  

\[
\begin{cases}
\mu ^{T}\beta =\sigma\\[1mm]
\mathbf 1^{T}\beta =1
\end{cases}
\Longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
\lambda a-\nu b = 2\sigma ,\\[1mm]
\lambda b-\nu c = 2 .
\end{cases}
\]

Solving,

\[
\boxed{\;
\lambda =\frac{2c\,\sigma-2b}{\Delta},\qquad
\nu     =\frac{\lambda b-2}{c}
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

and the optimal vector is  

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{*}= \frac12\,M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1\bigr)
\;}
\tag{6}
\]

provided that \(\beta^{*}\ge 0\).  If some components of (6) are negative,
those components are set to zero, the corresponding \(\alpha_i\) become
strictly positive, and the system is resolved on the reduced active set
(standard active‑set algorithm).

---

### 4.  Final form of the solution  

The optimal solution is the **projection of the origin onto the feasible
polytope \(C\) in the norm induced by \(M\)**,

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{*}= \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\beta\in C}\; \beta^{T}M\beta
          \;=\; \Pi^{M}_{C}(0)
\;}
\]

and can be obtained by solving the KKT system above.  In practice one
uses the case analysis (a)–(d) or an active‑set / interior‑point QP
solver; the explicit expressions (2)–(6) give the solution whenever the
set of active constraints is known.  The multipliers \(\lambda,\nu,
\alpha\) are given by (5) and (3) respectively.  

Thus the problem is completely solved by the KKT conditions; the
solution is unique when \(M\) is positive‑definite.

Solution 1:
**Solution by the KKT‐conditions**

The problem  

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{p}} & f(\beta)=\beta^{\top}M\beta \\[1ex]
\text{s.t.} & g_{1}(\beta)=\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta\;\le 0,\\
            & g_{2}(\beta)=\mathbf 1^{\top}\beta-1\;\le 0,\\
            & g_{3,i}(\beta)=-\beta_{i}\;\le 0,\qquad i=1,\dots ,p ,
\end{array}
\]

is a convex quadratic program (assume \(M\succeq0\)).  
Introduce non‑negative Lagrange multipliers  

\[
\lambda_{1}\ge0,\qquad \lambda_{2}\ge0,\qquad 
\lambda_{3}=(\lambda_{3,1},\dots ,\lambda_{3,p})^{\top}\ge0 .
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda)=\beta^{\top}M\beta 
+\lambda_{1}\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta\bigr)
+\lambda_{2}\bigl(\mathbf1^{\top}\beta-1\bigr)
+\lambda_{3}^{\top}(-\beta).
\]

---

### 1. KKT conditions  

* **Stationarity**

\[
\nabla_\beta\mathcal L=2M\beta-\lambda_{1}\mu+\lambda_{2}\mathbf1-\lambda_{3}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
2M\beta=\lambda_{1}\mu-\lambda_{2}\mathbf1+\lambda_{3}. \tag{1}
\]

* **Primal feasibility**  

\[
\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta\le0,\qquad 
\mathbf1^{\top}\beta-1\le0,\qquad 
-\beta_i\le0 .
\]

* **Dual feasibility**  

\[
\lambda_{1}\ge0,\quad \lambda_{2}\ge0,\quad \lambda_{3,i}\ge0 .
\]

* **Complementary slackness**

\[
\lambda_{1}\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta\bigr)=0,\qquad
\lambda_{2}\bigl(\mathbf1^{\top}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\qquad
\lambda_{3,i}(-\beta_i)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_{3,i}\beta_i=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 2. Form of the solution  

Let  

\[
\mathcal S=\{i\mid\beta_i>0\}
\]

be the **support** of the optimal vector.  
For \(i\in\mathcal S\) we have \(\lambda_{3,i}=0\) by (2).  
Hence on the support (1) becomes  

\[
2M_{\mathcal S\mathcal S}\beta_{\mathcal S}
=\lambda_{1}\mu_{\mathcal S}-\lambda_{2}\mathbf1_{\mathcal S},
\tag{3}
\]

where the subscript \(\mathcal S\mathcal S\) denotes the sub‑matrix of
\(M\) with rows and columns indexed by \(\mathcal S\), and
\(\beta_{\mathcal S},\mu_{\mathcal S},\mathbf1_{\mathcal S}\) are the
corresponding subvectors.

Assuming \(\mathcal S\) is known and that
\(M_{\mathcal S\mathcal S}\) is invertible, (3) gives

\[
\beta_{\mathcal S}
=\frac12\,M_{\mathcal S\mathcal S}^{-1}
\bigl(\lambda_{1}\mu_{\mathcal S}-\lambda_{2}\mathbf1_{\mathcal S}\bigr).
\tag{4}
\]

The two linear constraints are either active (tight) or not.
Because the objective is strictly convex, at the optimum at least one
of them must be active.  
The possible cases are:

| active constraints | consequence for multipliers | expression for \(\beta\) |
|--------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------|
| only \(\mu^{\top}\beta\ge\sigma\) | \(\lambda_{1}>0,\;\lambda_{2}=0\) | \(\displaystyle\beta=\frac{\sigma}{c_{1}}\,M^{-1}\mu\) |
| only \(\mathbf1^{\top}\beta\le1\) | \(\lambda_{1}=0,\;\lambda_{2}>0\) | \(\displaystyle\beta=\frac{1}{c_{3}}\,M^{-1}\mathbf1\) |
| both are active | \(\lambda_{1}>0,\;\lambda_{2}>0\) | see below |

where  

\[
c_{1}= \mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu,\qquad 
c_{2}= \mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf1,\qquad 
c_{3}= \mathbf1^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf1 .
\tag{5}
\]

---

#### 2.1  Only the mean‑constraint active  

If the candidate  

\[
\beta^{(a)}\;=\;\frac{\sigma}{c_{1}}\,M^{-1}\mu                                 \tag{6}
\]

satisfies  

\[
\mathbf1^{\top}\beta^{(a)}\le1,\qquad \beta^{(a)}\ge0,
\]

then (6) is optimal.  In this case the Lagrange multiplier is  

\[
\lambda_{1}= \frac{2\sigma}{c_{1}},\qquad\lambda_{2}=0 .
\]

---

#### 2.2  Both linear constraints active  

Assume now that \(\beta^{(a)}\) violates at least one of the
non‑negativity or sum constraints.  
Then we must have \(\lambda_{1}>0,\;\lambda_{2}>0\) and (4) with  
\(\mathcal S=\{1,\dots ,p\}\) (i.e. all components are strictly positive)
holds.  Substituting (4) into the two tight constraints  

\[
\mu^{\top}\beta=\sigma,\qquad \mathbf1^{\top}\beta=1
\]

gives a linear system for \(\lambda_{1}\) and \(\lambda_{2}\):

\[
\frac12
\begin{bmatrix}
c_{1} & -c_{2}\\[0.2ex]
c_{2} & -c_{3}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}\\ \lambda_{2}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Solving, using \(\Delta=c_{1}c_{3}-c_{2}^{2}>0\) (which holds because
\(M^{-1}\) is positive definite), yields  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{1}&= \frac{2\bigl(c_{3}\sigma-c_{2}\bigr)}{\Delta},\\[0.4ex]
\lambda_{2}&= \frac{2\bigl(c_{1}-c_{2}\sigma\bigr)}{\Delta}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{7}
\]

Inserting (7) into (4) gives the **closed‑form candidate** when both
constraints are binding:

\[
\boxed{
\beta^{(b)}=
\frac{1}{\Delta}\,
M^{-1}\Bigl[\bigl(c_{3}\sigma-c_{2}\bigr)\,\mu
-\bigl(c_{1}-c_{2}\sigma\bigr)\,\mathbf1\Bigr] } . \tag{8}
\]

If all components of \(\beta^{(b)}\) are non‑negative, then
\(\beta^{(b)}\) is the optimal solution.

---

#### 2.3  Handling non‑negativity  

If some components of \(\beta^{(b)}\) are negative, the corresponding
indices belong to the *inactive* set (they must be set to zero).  
Let  

\[
\mathcal A=\{i\mid\beta^{(b)}_{i}<0\},\qquad 
\mathcal S=\{1,\dots ,p\}\setminus\mathcal A .
\]

Fix \(\beta_i=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal A\) (so \(\lambda_{3,i}>0\) there) and
repeat the derivation **restricted to the reduced support \(\mathcal S\)**
(see (3)–(4)).  This yields a new linear system for the two multipliers
\(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\) that involves the sub‑matrices
\(M_{\mathcal S\mathcal S}\), \(\mu_{\mathcal S}\), \(\mathbf1_{\mathcal S}\).
The procedure (often called an *active‑set* or *primal‑dual*
algorithm) is repeated until the computed \(\beta_{\mathcal S}\) is
non‑negative.  Because the problem is convex, this finite procedure
converges to the global optimum.

---

### 3. Summary of the solution  

1. Compute the three scalar quantities (5).  
2. **Try the one‑constraint solution** (6).  
   *If* \(\mathbf1^{\top}\beta^{(a)}\le1\) **and** \(\beta^{(a)}\ge0\) **then**  

   \[
   \boxed{\;\beta^{\star}= \beta^{(a)}=\frac{\sigma}{\mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu}\,
          M^{-1}\mu\;}
   \]

   is optimal.  

3. **Otherwise** solve the two‑constraint system (8).  
   *If* all components of \(\beta^{(b)}\) are non‑negative, set  

   \[
   \boxed{\;\beta^{\star}= \beta^{(b)}=
          \frac{ M^{-1}\bigl[(c_{3}\sigma-c_{2})\mu-(c_{1}-c_{2}\sigma)\mathbf1\bigr] }
               {c_{1}c_{3}-c_{2}^{2}}\;}
   \]

   (with the multipliers given by (7)).  

4. **If** some entries of \(\beta^{(b)}\) are negative,
   eliminate those indices (set the corresponding \(\beta_i\) to zero)
   and resolve the reduced problem by repeating step 3 on the
   remaining variables.  The resulting vector satisfies all KKT
   conditions and is the global minimiser \(\beta^{\star}\).

Because the objective is convex and the feasible set is a closed convex
polyhedron, the \(\beta^{\star}\) obtained by the above KKT‑procedure is
the unique global optimum of the original problem.  

\[
\boxed{
\displaystyle 
\beta^{\star}= 
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\sigma}{\mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu}\,M^{-1}\mu,
 & \text{if } \displaystyle
\frac{\sigma}{\mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu}\,
\mathbf1^{\top}M^{-1}\mu\le1\ \text{and}\ \beta^{\star}\ge0,\\[2.0ex]
\displaystyle\frac{ M^{-1}\bigl[(c_{3}\sigma-c_{2})\mu-
                (c_{1}-c_{2}\sigma)\mathbf1\bigr] }
               {c_{1}c_{3}-c_{2}^{2}}, & \text{otherwise (with possible
               zero‑components obtained by an active‑set refinement).}
\end{cases}}
\]  

where \(c_{1}= \mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu,\;c_{2}= \mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf1,\;
c_{3}= \mathbf1^{\top}M^{-1}\mathbf1\).  If \(M\) is singular, replace
\(M^{-1}\) by the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse \(M^{\dagger}\).

Solution 2:
**Solution**

The problem is a convex quadratic program (the objective is quadratic and the feasible set is a polyhedron).  
Let  

\[
\beta\in\mathbb R^{p},\qquad 
M\in\mathbb R^{p\times p},\;M\succeq0 ,\qquad 
\mu\in\mathbb R^{p},\qquad 
\sigma>0 .
\]

Introduce the Lagrange multipliers  

\[
\lambda\ge 0 \;( \text{for } \mu^{\!T}\beta\ge\sigma),\qquad
\nu\ge 0 \;( \text{for } 1^{\!T}\beta\le 1),\qquad
\omega\in\mathbb R^{p}_{+}\;( \text{for } \beta\ge0).
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\omega)=\beta^{T}M\beta
-\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)
+\nu\bigl(1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)-\omega^{T}\beta .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  KKT conditions  

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{(stationarity)} & 2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\omega=0,\\[2mm]
\text{(primal feasibility)} &
\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma,\;1^{T}\beta\le1,\;\beta\ge0,\\[1mm]
\text{(dual feasibility)} &
\lambda\ge0,\;\nu\ge0,\;\omega\ge0,\\[1mm]
\text{(complementary slackness)} &
\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)=0,\;
\nu\bigl(1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\;
\omega_i\beta_i=0\;(i=1,\dots,p).
\end{cases}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Structure of the optimal solution  

If a component \(\beta_i>0\) then, by complementary slackness, \(\omega_i=0\).  
Thus for every index \(i\) with \(\beta_i>0\)

\[
\bigl[2M\beta\frown}_{i}= \lambda\mu_i-\nu .
\]

Collect the set of active indices  

\[
\mathcal A:=\{i\mid\beta_i>0\}\qquad(\text{so }\beta_{\mathcal A^c}=0).
\]

Restricting the stationarity equation to \(\mathcal A\) gives  

\[
2M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}\,\beta_{\mathcal A}
   =\lambda\mu_{\mathcal A}-\nu\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A},
\qquad
\beta_{\mathcal A}
   =\frac12 M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}
      \bigl(\lambda\mu_{\mathcal A}-\nu\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

Hence the optimal vector can be written as  

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{*}= 
\bigl[\tfrac12 M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}
      (\lambda^{*}\mu_{\mathcal A}-\nu^{*}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A})\bigr]_{\!+\;0},
\;}
\tag{2}
\]

where \([\,\cdot\,]_{+0}\) means that the components belonging to \(\mathcal A\) are given by (1) and the remaining components are set to zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determination of the multipliers  

Only the **binding** inequality constraints can have a strictly positive multiplier.  
Consequently three cases can occur:

| Binding constraints | Multipliers | Determination of \(\lambda^{*},\nu^{*}\) |
|----------------------|------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Both** \(\mu^{T}\beta=\sigma\) and \(1^{T}\beta=1\) | \(\lambda>0,\;\nu>0\) | Insert (1) into the two equalities and solve the linear system  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}&=\sigma,\\
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}&=1,
\end{aligned}
\]
which yields  

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A} &
-\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}\\[2mm]
-\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}&
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda^{*}\\ \nu^{*}\end{bmatrix}
=2\begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
\] |
| **Only** \(\mu^{T}\beta=\sigma\) (the sum‑constraint is slack) | \(\lambda>0,\;\nu=0\) | From (1) with \(\nu=0\),

\[
\beta_{\mathcal A}= \frac{\lambda}{2}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A},
\qquad
\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}= \frac{\lambda}{2}
      \mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}= \sigma,
\]

hence  

\[
\lambda^{*}= \frac{2\sigma}
{\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}},\qquad
\nu^{*}=0 .
\] |
| **Only** \(1^{T}\beta=1\) (the mean‑constraint is slack) | \(\lambda=0,\;\nu>0\) | Analogous to the previous line,  

\[
\beta_{\mathcal A}= -\frac{\nu}{2}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A},
\qquad
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}= -\frac{\nu}{2}
      \mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}=1,
\]

so  

\[
\nu^{*}= -\frac{2}
{\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}},\qquad
\lambda^{*}=0 .
\] |

If the solution obtained from the above formulas yields any component \(\beta_i<0\), the corresponding index must be removed from \(\mathcal A\) and the calculation repeated. Because the objective is strictly convex (when \(M\succ0\)) this procedure converges after at most \(p\) iterations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Final compact expression  

Putting everything together, the optimal vector is the **projection** of the unconstrained minimiser onto the feasible polyhedron:

\[
\boxed{
\;
\beta^{*}= \underset{\beta\ge0,\;\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma,\;1^{T}\beta\le1}
{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\beta^{T}M\beta
=
\bigl[\tfrac12 M^{-1}(\lambda^{*}\mu-\nu^{*}\mathbf 1)\bigr]_{+0},
\;}
\]

where the non‑negative scalars \(\lambda^{*},\nu^{*}\) are obtained from the linear system that corresponds to the set of constraints that are active at optimality (as described in the table above).  

In other words, solve the KKT conditions; the solution is given by (2) with the multipliers \(\lambda^{*},\nu^{*}\) determined by whichever of the two linear constraints are tight. This \(\beta^{*}\) is the unique global minimiser of the original problem.

Solution 3:
Below is a complete, step‑by‑step derivation of the optimal solution of the quadratic program  

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle \min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{p}} & \beta^{\!T}M\beta \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} & \mu^{\!T}\beta\;\ge \sigma,\\
            & {\bf 1}^{\!T}\beta\;\le 1,\\
            & \beta_i\ge 0,\; i=1,\dots ,p .
\end{array}
\tag{P}
\]

(Throughout we assume that the matrix \(M\) is symmetric and positive‑semidefinite, so that the objective is convex.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Lagrangian and KKT conditions  

Introduce the Lagrange multipliers  

* \(\lambda\ge 0\) for the inequality \(\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma\);
* \(\nu \ge 0\) for the inequality \({\bf 1}^{T}\beta\le 1\);
* \(\gamma=(\gamma_1,\dots ,\gamma_p)^{T}\) with \(\gamma_i\ge 0\) for the non‑negativity constraints \(\beta_i\ge0\).

The Lagrangian of (P) is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\gamma)=\beta^{T}M\beta 
      -\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)
      +\nu\bigl({\bf 1}^{T}\beta-1\bigr)
      -\gamma^{T}\beta .
\]

The Karush‑Kuhn‑Tucker (KKT) conditions are

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{(i) Stationarity: }&& 2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu{\bf 1}-\gamma =0,\\[2pt]
&\text{(ii) Primal feasibility: }&& 
   \mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma,\qquad {\bf 1}^{T}\beta\le 1,\qquad \beta\ge 0,\\[2pt]
&\text{(iii) Dual feasibility: }&& \lambda\ge0,\ \nu\ge0,\ \gamma\ge0,\\[2pt]
&\text{(iv) Complementarity: }&&
   \lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)=0,\qquad 
   \nu\bigl({\bf 1}^{T}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\qquad 
   \gamma_i\beta_i =0\;(i=1,\dots ,p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{KKT}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Structure of the optimal \(\beta\)

From (i) we obtain  

\[
\beta = \tfrac12 M^{\dagger}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf 1}+\gamma\bigr),
\tag{1}
\]

where \(M^{\dagger}\) denotes the (Moore–Penrose) pseudoinverse of \(M\)
(the inverse if \(M\) is nonsingular).  

Because \(\gamma_i\beta_i=0\) (complementarity), each component of \(\beta\) falls into one of two mutually exclusive cases:

| case | condition on \(\beta_i\) | multiplier \(\gamma_i\) |
|------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| **A** | \(\beta_i>0\)            | \(\gamma_i=0\)          |
| **B** | \(\beta_i=0\)            | \(\gamma_i\ge 0\) (free) |

Consequently, for the indices that belong to **A** we have from (1)  

\[
\beta_i = \frac12\bigl(M^{\dagger}(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf 1})\bigr)_i ,
\qquad i\in A.
\tag{2}
\]

For the indices in **B**, the KKT stationarity condition reduces to  

\[
\bigl(2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu{\bf 1}\bigr)_i \;=\;\gamma_i\;\ge 0 .
\tag{3}
\]

Thus the optimal \(\beta\) is **the projection of the unconstrained minimiser**  

\[
\beta^{\text{unc}}(\lambda,\nu)
      \;:=\;\frac12M^{\dagger}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf 1}\bigr)
\tag{4}
\]

onto the non‑negative orthant, while simultaneously satisfying the two scalar constraints
\(\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma\) and \({\bf 1}^{T}\beta\le 1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determining the multipliers \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\)

Because the objective is strictly convex when \(M\succ 0\), the optimal
pair \((\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\) is unique and can be found by solving the scalar
complementarity equations

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda^\star\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta^{\star}-\sigma\bigr)&=0,\\[4pt]
\nu^\star\bigl({\bf 1}^{T}\beta^{\star}-1\bigr)&=0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

with \(\beta^{\star}\) given by the projection described in the previous section.
Equation (5) leads to three possible regimes:

1. **Both constraints inactive** (\(\lambda^\star=0,\ \nu^\star=0\)).  
   Then \(\beta^{\star}={\bf 0}\). This is feasible only if \(\sigma\le 0\) and the
   inequality \({\bf 1}^{T}{\bf 0}=0\le1\) holds.

2. **Only the mean‑return constraint active** (\(\lambda^\star>0,\ \nu^\star=0\)).  
   Here \(\beta^{\star}= \tfrac12M^{-1}\lambda^\star\mu\) (projected onto \(\beta\ge0\)).  
   The multiplier is chosen so that the active constraint holds with equality:
   \[
   \mu^{T}\beta^{\star}= \sigma .
   \tag{6}
   \]

3. **Only the budget constraint active** (\(\lambda^\star=0,\ \nu^\star>0\)).  
   Then \(\beta^{\star}= -\tfrac12M^{-1}\nu^\star{\bf 1}\) (projected onto the non‑negative orthant).  
   The multiplier satisfies
   \[
   {\bf 1}^{T}\beta^{\star}=1 .
   \tag{7}
   \]

4. **Both constraints active** (\(\lambda^\star>0,\ \nu^\star>0\)).  
   In this case \(\beta^{\star}\) satisfies both equalities
   \[
   \mu^{T}\beta^{\star}= \sigma , \qquad {\bf 1}^{T}\beta^{\star}=1 .
   \tag{8}
   \]
   Substituting \(\beta^{\star}\) from (4) (without the non‑negativity projection) gives a
   linear system for \(\lambda^\star,\nu^\star\):
   \[
   \begin{bmatrix}
      \mu^{T}M^{-1}\mu & -\mu^{T}M^{-1}{\bf 1}\\[4pt]
      -{\bf 1}^{T}M^{-1}\mu & {\bf 1}^{T}M^{-1}{\bf 1}
   \end{bmatrix}
   \begin{bmatrix}
      \lambda^\star\\ \nu^\star
   \end{bmatrix}
   = 2\begin{bmatrix}
      \sigma \\ 1
   \end{bmatrix}.
   \tag{9}
   \]
   Provided the solution of (9) yields \(\lambda^\star,\nu^\star\ge0\) and the resulting
   \(\beta^{\star}\) is component‑wise non‑negative, this is the optimal point.

Hence the optimal multiplier vector \((\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\) is obtained by
checking the four regimes above in the order: (i) both inactive,
(ii) only \(\lambda\) active, (iii) only \(\nu\) active, (iv) both active,
and selecting the first feasible one.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Closed‑form expression of the optimum  

Putting the above pieces together, the optimal solution can be written compactly as  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\beta^\star \;=\;&\Pi_{\mathbb R^{p}_{+}}\!\Bigl(
        \tfrac12 M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda^\star\mu-\nu^\star{\bf 1}\bigr)
        \Bigr) ,\\[4pt]
\text{where }(\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\;&\text{solve the KKT system }(5)\text{ and belong to one of the four regimes described above.}
\end{aligned}}
\]

Here \(\Pi_{\mathbb R^{p}_{+}}(\cdot)\) denotes Euclidean projection onto the non‑negative orthant (i.e. setting any negative component to zero).  

In the **generic case** when the solution of the linear system (9) yields non‑negative multipliers and a non‑negative vector, the explicit optimal weights are

\[
\boxed{
\beta^\star \;=\;
\Pi_{\mathbb R^{p}_{+}}\!\Bigl(
\frac12 M^{-1}
\bigl(\lambda^\star\mu-\nu^\star{\bf 1}\bigr)
\Bigr),\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda^\star\\ \nu^\star
\end{bmatrix}
=
2\begin{bmatrix}
\mu^{T}M^{-1}\mu & -\mu^{T}M^{-1}{\bf 1}\\[4pt]
-{\bf 1}^{T}M^{-1}\mu & {\bf 1}^{T}M^{-1}{\bf 1}
\end{bmatrix}^{\!{-1}}
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma \\ 1
\end{bmatrix}.}
\]

If the multipliers obtained from the matrix inverse are not both non‑negative,
or if the resulting vector has negative components, the appropriate
boundary regime (only one active constraint or the trivial solution
\(\beta=0\)) must be used, with \(\lambda^\star\) or \(\nu^\star\) set to zero and the remaining multiplier determined from the single active equality
(\(\mu^{T}\beta=\sigma\) or \({\bf 1}^{T}\beta=1\)) together with the non‑negativity projection.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Summary  

The quadratic program is convex, so the KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient.
The optimal weight vector \(\beta^\star\) is obtained by:

1. Solving the 2×2 linear system (9) for the Lagrange multipliers;
2. Checking the sign of the multipliers and the non‑negativity of the resulting
   \(\beta\);
3. If they satisfy the required signs, the solution is given by the projected
   expression above; otherwise, one (or both) of the scalar constraints is
   inactive and the corresponding multiplier(s) is set to zero, after which the
   remaining multiplier is found from the single active equality, again
   followed by projection onto the non‑negative orthant.

This provides a complete, closed‑form description of the optimal solution to the problem.

Solution 4:
**Step 1 – Lagrangian and KKT conditions**

\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\beta,\lambda ,\nu ,\omega )
&= \beta^{\!T}M\beta 
   +\lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\!T}\beta\bigr)   
   +\nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\beta-1\bigr)   
   +\omega^{\!T}(-\beta) ,\\[2mm]
\lambda&\ge 0,\; \nu\ge 0,\; \omega_i\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

*Stationarity*  

\[
\nabla_{\beta}L=2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\omega=0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\beta=\tfrac12M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1+\omega\bigr). \tag{1}
\]

*Complementarity*  

\[
\lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\!T}\beta\bigr)=0,\qquad
\nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\qquad
\omega_i\beta_i=0\;(i=1,\dots ,p). \tag{2}
\]

*Primal feasibility*  

\[
\mu^{\!T}\beta\ge\sigma,\qquad 
\mathbf 1^{\!T}\beta\le1,\qquad 
\beta\ge0. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2 – Eliminate the non‑negativity multipliers**

Let  

\[
S:=\{i\mid\beta_i>0\}
\]

be the set of indices that are strictly positive at the optimum.  
For \(i\in S\) we have \(\omega_i=0\) (by (2)), whereas for \(i\notin S\) we set \(\beta_i=0\) and keep \(\omega_i\ge0\).

Restrict (1) to the active set \(S\) (hence \(\omega_S=0\)):

\[
\beta_S \;=\;\frac12M_{SS}^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu_S-\nu\mathbf1_S\bigr),\tag{4}
\]

where the subscript \(SS\) denotes the principal sub‑matrix of \(M\) indexed by \(S\) and
\(\mu_S,\mathbf1_S\) are the corresponding subvectors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3 – Determine which scalar constraints are binding**

Because the objective is convex (\(M\succeq0\)), an optimal solution will satisfy at least one of the scalar constraints with equality.  
Three possibilities have to be examined:

1. **Both constraints bind** (\(\lambda>0,\;\nu>0\)).  
   Then \(\mu_S^{\!T}\beta_S=\sigma\) and \(\mathbf1_S^{\!T}\beta_S=1\).  
   Substituting (4) gives the linear system  

   \[
   \begin{cases}
   \lambda\,A_S-\nu\,B_S=2\sigma,\\[1mm]
   \lambda\,B_S-\nu\,C_S=2,
   \end{cases}\qquad 
   \begin{aligned}
   A_S&:=\mu_S^{\!T}M_{SS}^{-1}\mu_S,\\
   B_S&:=\mu_S^{\!T}M_{SS}^{-1}\mathbf1_S,\\
   C_S&:=\mathbf1_S^{\!T}M_{SS}^{-1}\mathbf1_S .
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   Solving,
   \[
   \boxed{\;
   \lambda
   =\frac{2\bigl(B_S-\sigma C_S\bigr)}{B_S^{2}-A_S C_S},
   \qquad
   \nu
   =\frac{2\bigl(A_S-\sigma B_S\bigr)}{B_S^{2}-A_S C_S}\;}. \tag{5}
   \]

   Inserting (5) into (4) yields the optimal weights on the active set:

   \[
   \boxed{\;
   \beta_S^{*}
   =\frac{M_{SS}^{-1}\Bigl[(B_S-\sigma C_S)\,\mu_S-(A_S-\sigma B_S)\,\mathbf1_S\Bigr]}
          {\,B_S^{2}-A_S C_S\,}\;}. \tag{6}
   \]

2. **Only the return constraint binds** (\(\lambda>0,\;\nu=0\)).  
   Then (4) together with \(\mu_S^{\!T}\beta_S=\sigma\) gives  

   \[
   \lambda A_S=2\sigma\;\Longrightarrow\;
   \lambda=\frac{2\sigma}{A_S},\qquad
   \beta_S^{*}= \frac{\sigma}{A_S}\,M_{SS}^{-1}\mu_S .
   \]

3. **Only the budget constraint binds** (\(\lambda=0,\;\nu>0\)).  
   Analogously  

   \[
   \nu C_S=2\;\Longrightarrow\;
   \nu=\frac{2}{C_S},\qquad
   \beta_S^{*}= \frac{1}{C_S}\,M_{SS}^{-1}\mathbf1_S .
   \]

If none of the scalar constraints is active, the only feasible point is \(\beta=0\) (which can satisfy the problem only when \(\sigma\le0\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4 – Enforce non‑negativity**

The expression (6) (or the special‑case formulas) must be checked component‑wise.
If any component of the candidate \(\beta_S^{*}\) is negative, that index cannot belong to the active set.  
Remove all indices with negative weight, call the reduced set \(\tilde S\), and resolve the appropriate case on \(\tilde S\).  
Because every iteration eliminates at least one index, the procedure terminates in at most \(p\) steps and returns the unique global minimiser (the problem is convex).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Final solution**

Let \(S^{*}\subseteq\{1,\dots ,p\}\) be the set of indices that remain after the above active‑set elimination.  
Define the scalars

\[
A:=\mu_{S^{*}}^{\!T}M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\mu_{S^{*}},\qquad
B:=\mu_{S^{*}}^{\!T}M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\mathbf1_{S^{*}},\qquad
C:=\mathbf1_{S^{*}}^{\!T}M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\mathbf1_{S^{*}} .
\]

If both constraints are binding (the generic case) the optimal weight vector is  

\[
\boxed{
\beta^{*}_i=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{\bigl[(B-\sigma C)\,\mu_i-(A-\sigma B)\bigr]}
      {\,B^{2}-AC\,}\;\bigl[M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\bigr]_{i\bullet},
& i\in S^{*},\\[3mm]
0, & i\notin S^{*},
\end{cases}
}
\]

where \([M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}]_{i\bullet}\) denotes the \(i\)-th row of the inverse of the sub‑matrix of \(M\) corresponding to \(S^{*}\).  

If only the return (resp. the budget) constraint is active, replace the numerator in the above formula by \(\sigma\,M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\mu_{S^{*}}\) (resp. \(M_{S^{*}S^{*}}^{-1}\mathbf1_{S^{*}}\)) and the denominator by \(A\) (resp. \(C\)).  

The vector \(\beta^{*}\) thus obtained satisfies all the original constraints and minimizes \(\beta^{\!T}M\beta\).  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\beta^{*}\;=\;\arg\min_{\beta\ge0,\; \mu^{\!T}\beta\ge\sigma,\;\mathbf1^{\!T}\beta\le1}\beta^{\!T}M\beta
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
\text{(6) on the active set }S^{*},\\[2mm]
\text{or the reduced‑case formulas if one scalar constraint is non‑binding.}
\end{cases}}
\]

Solution 5:
Below is a complete derivation of the optimal vector \(\boldsymbol\beta^{\star}\).  
All steps are written out so that the answer can be verified and used directly in a numerical routine.

---

### 1.  Problem statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^{p}} \;&\; f(\boldsymbol\beta)=\boldsymbol\beta^{\!T}\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta  \\
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\;\geq\;\sigma,\\[4pt]
\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\;\leq\;1,\\[4pt]
\boldsymbol\beta\;\geq\;\mathbf 0 .
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

Assume that \(\mathbf M\) is **positive‑definite** (the case of a positive‑semi‑definite matrix is treated analogously by using a pseudoinverse).  
Hence the problem is a convex quadratic programme.

---

### 2.  Lagrangian and KKT conditions  

Introduce Lagrange multipliers  

* \(\lambda\ge 0\)   for the constraint \(\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\ge\sigma\)
* \(\nu   \ge 0\)   for the constraint \(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\le1\)
* \(\boldsymbol\gamma\ge\mathbf 0\)   for the componentwise non‑negativity \(\boldsymbol\beta\ge\mathbf0\).

The Lagrangian (written with the constraints in the standard “\(\le\)” form) is  

\[
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta,\lambda,\nu,\boldsymbol\gamma)=
\boldsymbol\beta^{\!T}\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta
+ \lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\bigr)
+ \nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta-1\bigr)
-\boldsymbol\gamma^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta .
\]

The KKT conditions are  

| (i) Primal feasibility | \(\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\ge\sigma,\; \mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta\le1,\; \boldsymbol\beta\ge\mathbf0\) |
|---|---|
| (ii) Dual feasibility | \(\lambda\ge0,\; \nu\ge0,\; \boldsymbol\gamma\ge\mathbf0\) |
| (iii) Complementary slackness | \(\lambda(\sigma-\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta)=0,\;\nu(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta-1)=0,\;\gamma_i\beta_i=0\;\;(i=1,\dots,p)\) |
| (iv) Stationarity | \(\displaystyle 2\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\boldsymbol\gamma=\mathbf 0.\) |

---

### 3.  Solving the stationarity condition  

From (iv) we have  

\[
2\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta = \lambda\mu - \nu\mathbf 1 + \boldsymbol\gamma . \tag{1}
\]

If a component \(\beta_i>0\) then, by complementary slackness, \(\gamma_i=0\).  
Thus for every **active** index (i.e. whose \(\beta_i>0\))

\[
\bigl[2\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta\bigr]_i = \lambda\mu_i - \nu . \tag{2}
\]

If \(\beta_i=0\) we only know that  

\[
\bigl[2\mathbf M\boldsymbol\beta\bigr]_i \ \ge\ \lambda\mu_i - \nu ,
\]

because \(\gamma_i\ge0\).  

Consequently, when the set of active indices is known, (2) can be written in matrix form as  

\[
2\mathbf M_{AA}\,\boldsymbol\beta_A = \lambda\mu_A - \nu\mathbf 1_A , \tag{3}
\]

where the subscript \(A\) denotes the rows/columns belonging to the active set.  
If the active set contains *all* indices (\(\beta_i>0\;\forall i\)), then \(\boldsymbol\gamma=\mathbf0\) and (1) simplifies to  

\[
\boxed{\;\boldsymbol\beta
      =\frac12\mathbf M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1\bigr)\;}. \tag{4}
\]

Thus the whole problem reduces to finding the two scalars \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\).

---

### 4.  Determining \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\)

Two of the constraints can be **tight** (active) at the optimum; the remaining ones are either slack (multiplier = 0) or also tight.  
We therefore have three possibilities:

| Active constraints | Multipliers | Resulting equations for \(\lambda,\nu\) |
|---|---|---|
| **Both** \(\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta=\sigma\) and \(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta=1\) | \(\lambda>0,\;\nu>0\) | Using (4) in the two equalities gives the linear system  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\mu^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu & -\mu^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1\\[4pt]
\mathbf 1^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu & -\mathbf 1^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\ \nu\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}2\sigma\\ 2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{5}
\] |
| **Only** \(\mu^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta=\sigma\) (the sum‑constraint is slack) | \(\lambda>0,\;\nu=0\) | \(\displaystyle \lambda
   = \frac{2\sigma}{\mu^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu},\qquad
   \boldsymbol\beta = \frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu.
\) |
| **Only** \(\mathbf 1^{\!T}\boldsymbol\beta=1\) (the \(\mu\)-constraint is slack) | \(\lambda=0,\;\nu>0\) | \(\displaystyle \nu
   = \frac{2}{\mathbf 1^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1},
   \qquad\boldsymbol\beta = \frac{\nu}{2}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1.
\) |

The appropriate case is selected by checking the non‑negativity of the resulting \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and the sign conditions \(\lambda\ge0,\;\nu\ge0\).  
If the solution of (5) yields \(\lambda\ge0,\;\nu\ge0\) **and** \(\boldsymbol\beta\ge\mathbf0\), then (4) together with (5) gives the optimum.  

If in (5) either \(\lambda<0\) or \(\nu<0\), the corresponding multiplier must be set to zero and one of the two single‑constraint cases above is used.  

If after setting a multiplier to zero some components of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) become negative, those components are forced to zero, the associated \(\gamma_i\) becomes positive, and the linear system is re‑solved on the reduced active set (this is precisely the **active‑set** algorithm for quadratic programmes).

---

### 5.  Final closed‑form expression  

Putting everything together, the optimal vector is

\[
\boxed{\;
\boldsymbol\beta^{\star}
\;=\;
\max\!\Big\{\;
\mathbf 0,\;
\frac12\,\mathbf M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda^{\star}\mu-\nu^{\star}\mathbf 1\bigr)
\;\Big\}
\;}
\tag{6}
\]

where  

* \((\lambda^{\star},\nu^{\star})\) are the unique non‑negative solution of (5) **if** it yields a non‑negative \(\boldsymbol\beta\);  
* otherwise the pair is obtained from the single‑constraint formulas  

\[
\lambda^{\star}= \frac{2\sigma}{\mu^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu},\;\nu^{\star}=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\lambda^{\star}=0,\;\nu^{\star}= \frac{2}{\mathbf 1^{\!T}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1},
\]

whichever satisfies the remaining constraints.  

If some components of the vector returned by (6) are zero, the above procedure is repeated on the reduced set of indices (standard active‑set/QP solver).  

---

### 6.  Remarks  

* The problem is a **convex quadratic program**; any QP solver (e.g. interior‑point, active‑set, or specialised QP libraries) will return the same \(\boldsymbol\beta^{\star}\).  
* When \(\mathbf M\) is only positive‑semi‑definite, replace \(\mathbf M^{-1}\) by the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse \(\mathbf M^{\dagger}\) in the formulas above.  
* The closed‑form (6) together with the linear system (5) is the analytic solution when all constraints are active and the resulting vector is non‑negative.  

Thus the optimisation problem is completely solved.

Solution 6:
**Step 1 –  Write the problem in the standard convex‑QP form**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min _{\beta\in\mathbb R^{p}} && \tfrac12 \beta^{\!T} (2M)\beta  \\
\text{s.t. } && -\mu^{\!T}\beta \le -\sigma ,\\
&& \; \mathbf 1^{\!T}\beta \le 1 ,\\
&& -\beta \le 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The matrix \(2M\) is symmetric and, because the objective is a quadratic form,
the problem is convex provided that \(M\succeq0\) (positive‑semidefinite).  
Hence the Karush‑Kuhn‑Tucker (KKT) conditions are *necessary and sufficient* for optimality.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2 –  Introduce Lagrange multipliers**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &\ge 0 &&\text{(for }\mu^{T}\beta\ge \sigma\text{)}\\[2pt]
\nu &\ge 0 &&\text{(for }\mathbf 1^{T}\beta\le 1\text{)}\\[2pt]
\gamma &\in\mathbb R^{p},\;\gamma_i\ge 0 &&\text{(for } \beta_i\ge 0\text{)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\gamma)=\beta^{T}M\beta
-\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)
+\nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)
-\gamma^{T}\beta .
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3 –  Write the KKT system**

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{(stationarity)} & 2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\gamma=0,\\[4pt]
\text{(primal feasibility)} &
\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma,\;
\mathbf 1^{T}\beta\le 1,\;
\beta\ge0,\\[4pt]
\text{(dual feasibility)} &
\lambda\ge0,\;\nu\ge0,\;\gamma\ge0,\\[4pt]
\text{(complementary slackness)} &
\lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{T}\beta\bigr)=0,\;
\nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\;
\gamma_i\beta_i=0\;\;(i=1,\dots ,p).
\end{cases}
\tag{KKT}
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4 –  Solve the stationarity condition**

Assume that the matrix \(M\) is *positive‑definite* (hence invertible).  
From the first line of (KKT)

\[
\beta = M^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\mu-\tfrac{\nu}{2}\mathbf 1+\tfrac{1}{2}\gamma\Bigr). \tag{1}
\]

Because \(\gamma_i\beta_i=0\), each component of \(\gamma\) can be written as

\[
\gamma_i=
\begin{cases}
0, &\beta_i>0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle \bigl(2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1\bigr)_i\ge0, &\beta_i=0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the unknowns are the two scalars \(\lambda,\nu\) together with the *active set*
\(\mathcal A=\{i:\beta_i>0\}\).

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 5 –  Reduce to a low‑dimensional linear system**

Let \(\mathcal A\) be any candidate active set and denote by  
\(M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}\) the sub‑matrix of \(M\) formed by the rows and columns indexed by \(\mathcal A\), and by
\(\mu_{\mathcal A},\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}\) the corresponding subvectors.
If we temporarily assume that the constraints \(\beta_i\ge0\) are *inactive* for
\(i\in\mathcal A\) (i.e. \(\gamma_i=0\) there), (1) restricted to the active
coordinates gives

\[
\beta_{\mathcal A}= \frac{\lambda}{2}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}
-\frac{\nu}{2}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}. \tag{3}
\]

The two linear constraints become

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}&=\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}
M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}
-\frac{\nu}{2}\,\mu_{\mathcal A}^{T}
M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}\;\; \gtreqql\; \sigma ,\\[4pt]
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}\beta_{\mathcal A}&=\frac{\lambda}{2}\,
\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}
-\frac{\nu}{2}\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}^{T}
M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}\;\;\lteql\; 1 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

Because at optimum either the first or the second inequality is *tight*
(complementary slackness), we have two possibilities:

* **Case A** – the “return” constraint is active: \(\mu^{T}\beta=\sigma\) (so \(\lambda>0\));
* **Case B** – the “budget” constraint is active: \(\mathbf1^{T}\beta=1\) (so \(\nu>0\));
* **Case C** – both are active simultaneously (possible when the two
hyper‑planes intersect inside the simplex).

For a *given* active set \(\mathcal A\) we solve the 2×2 linear system that follows
from (4) together with the chosen active constraints.  This yields the unique
pair \((\lambda,\nu)\), and then \(\beta_{\mathcal A}\) is obtained from (3).  
Finally we check:

1. \(\beta_i\ge0\) for all \(i\in\mathcal A\) (by construction) and for
   \(i\notin\mathcal A\) we set \(\beta_i=0\);
2. The *non‑active* complementarity conditions (2) hold, i.e. the
   components of \(2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf1\) that correspond to the zero
   entries are non‑negative.

If the check succeeds, the candidate is the optimal solution.  
If not, a different active set must be tried.  Because the feasible region is
the (closed) simplex, only a finite number \((p+1)\) of active sets need be
examined, so the procedure terminates in a finite number of steps.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 6 –  Compact expression of the optimal solution**

Putting the above reasoning together, the optimal vector \(\beta^{\star}\) can be
written as  

\[
\boxed{
\beta^{\star}= M^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac{\lambda^{\star}}{2}\,\mu-\tfrac{\nu^{\star}}{2}\,
\mathbf 1+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\gamma^{\star}\bigr)
}
\]

where the scalars \(\lambda^{\star}\ge0,\;\nu^{\star}\ge0\) and the vector
\(\gamma^{\star}\ge0\) satisfy the KKT conditions listed in **Step 3**.  
Equivalently, one may describe the solution algorithmically as

```
for each candidate active set A ⊆ {1,…,p} do
    solve the 2×2 linear system obtained from (4) with the
    appropriate active constraints (μᵀβ = σ, 1ᵀβ = 1 or both);
    compute β_A from (3) and set β_i = 0 for i∉A;
    if β ≥ 0 and complementary slackness holds then
        return β as the optimum;
    end
end
```

Because the problem is a convex quadratic program, the β returned by the
first feasible active set encountered is the *global* minimizer.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Summary**

* The optimum exists and is unique when \(M\succ0\).  
* It is characterized completely by the KKT conditions  
  \(2M\beta^{\star}-\lambda^{\star}\mu+\nu^{\star}\mathbf1-\gamma^{\star}=0\) together
  with the primal, dual and complementary‑slackness constraints.  
* Practically, the solution can be obtained by enumerating the possible
  active sets of the non‑negativity constraints (a finite set) and solving the
  resulting small linear systems; this is exactly what any standard QP solver
  does.  

Thus the optimal \(\beta\) is given by the expression in the box above,
with \(\lambda^{\star},\nu^{\star},\gamma^{\star}\) determined from the KKT
conditions.

Solution 7:
The problem  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\beta\in\mathbb {R}^{p}} & \;\; \beta^{\top}M\beta \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } & \mu^{\top}\beta\;\ge \sigma ,\\
            & {\bf 1}^{\top}\beta\;\le 1 ,\\
            & \beta_i\ge 0 ,\;i=1,\dots ,p ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{P}
\]

is a convex quadratic program because the objective is a convex quadratic
(\(M\succeq0\)) and all constraints are linear.  
The optimal solution can be obtained from the Karush‑Kuhn‑Tucker (KKT)
conditions.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Lagrangian  

Introduce the Lagrange multipliers  

* \(\lambda\ge 0\) for the inequality \(\mu^{\top}\beta\ge\sigma\),  
* \(\nu\ge 0\) for the inequality \({\bf 1}^{\top}\beta\le 1\),  
* \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{p}_{+}\) for the non‑negativity constraints
  \(\beta_i\ge0\).

The Lagrangian (the factor \(1/2\) is omitted because the objective does not
contain it) is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\alpha)=\beta^{\top}M\beta
     -\lambda\bigl(\mu^{\top}\beta-\sigma\bigr)
     +\nu\bigl({\bf 1}^{\top}\beta-1\bigr)
     -\alpha^{\top}\beta .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  First‑order (stationarity) condition  

\[
\nabla_{\beta}\mathcal L=2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu{\bf 1}-\alpha =0 .
\tag{1}
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\;\beta = \tfrac{1}{2}\,M^{\dagger}
       \bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf 1}+\alpha\bigr)\;}
\tag{2}
\]

where \(M^{\dagger}\) denotes a (Moore–Penrose) generalized inverse of \(M\)
(the inverse if \(M\) is nonsingular).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Complementarity conditions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda\bigl(\mu^{\top}\beta-\sigma\bigr) &=0, \qquad  \lambda\ge0,
\\[1mm]
\nu\bigl({\bf 1}^{\top}\beta-1\bigr) &=0, \qquad  \nu\ge0,
\\[1mm]
\alpha_i\beta_i &=0 ,\qquad \alpha_i\ge0,\; \beta_i\ge0,\; i=1,\dots ,p .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Primal feasibility  

\[
\mu^{\top}\beta\ge\sigma,\qquad {\bf 1}^{\top}\beta\le 1,\qquad  
\beta_i\ge0 \;(i=1,\dots ,p). \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Solving the KKT system  

Let  

\[
\mathcal A:=\{\,i\mid \beta_i>0\,\}
\]

be the set of indices whose non‑negativity constraints are **inactive**.
For those components \(\alpha_i=0\) by (3).  
Define the *active* set  

\[
\mathcal I:=\{\,i\mid \beta_i =0\,\},
\qquad\text{so that }\;\alpha_i\ge0\;(i\in\mathcal I).
\]

Restrict (2) to the inactive coordinates:

\[
\beta_{\mathcal A}= \tfrac12\,M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}
       \bigl(\lambda\mu_{\mathcal A}-\nu{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}\bigr),
\tag{5}
\]

where \(M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}\) is the principal sub‑matrix of \(M\) indexed
by \(\mathcal A\), and \(\mu_{\mathcal A},{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}\) are the
corresponding subvectors.  
The two scalar multipliers \(\lambda,\nu\) are obtained from the two
remaining (possibly active) linear constraints:

\[
\begin{cases}
\mu_{\mathcal A}^{\top}\beta_{\mathcal A}= \sigma & \text{if }\lambda>0,
\\[1mm]
{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}^{\top}\beta_{\mathcal A}= 1   & \text{if }\nu>0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]

If a constraint is not active (its multiplier is zero) the corresponding
equality in (6) is dropped.  Consequently three cases have to be examined:

| Active constraints |  System to solve for \((\lambda,\nu)\) | \(\beta_{\mathcal A}\) |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|
| both \(\mu^{\top}\beta=\sigma\) and \({\bf 1}^{\top}\beta=1\) | \(\begin{bmatrix}\mu_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}& -\mu_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}\\[2mm]-{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}& {\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda\\ \nu\end{bmatrix}
=
2\begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\) | (5) |
| only \(\mu^{\top}\beta=\sigma\) | \(\lambda =\dfrac{2\sigma}{\mu_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}\mu_{\mathcal A}},\quad \nu=0\) | (5) |
| only \({\bf 1}^{\top}\beta=1\) | \(\nu =\dfrac{2}{ {\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}^{\top}M_{\mathcal A\mathcal A}^{-1}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal A}},\quad \lambda=0\) | (5) |

For each possible active‑set \(\mathcal A\) we compute \(\lambda,\nu\) from the
appropriate row of the table, obtain \(\beta_{\mathcal A}\) from (5) and set
\(\beta_i=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\).  The resulting vector is **feasible**
iff it satisfies (4) and the sign conditions \(\alpha_i\ge0\) for the
inactive constraints (which are equivalent to \(\lambda\mu_i-\nu\ge0\) for
\(i\in\mathcal I\)).  Among all feasible candidates we pick the one that gives
the smallest objective value \(\beta^{\top}M\beta\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Final result  

The optimal solution of the original problem is therefore the vector  

\[
\boxed{%
\beta^{\star}= \frac12\,M^{\dagger}
      \bigl(\lambda^{\star}\mu-\nu^{\star}{\bf 1}+\alpha^{\star}\bigr)
}
\tag{7}
\]

where the multipliers \(\lambda^{\star}\ge0,\;\nu^{\star}\ge0,\;
\alpha^{\star}\ge0\) together with the active index set \(\mathcal A\)
satisfy the KKT conditions (1)–(4).  In practice the solution is obtained
by enumerating the (typically small) set of active constraints, solving the
linear system (6) for each case, and selecting the feasible candidate with
minimum quadratic cost.  This is exactly the standard algorithm used by any
quadratic‑programming solver (interior‑point, active‑set, etc.).  

Thus the problem has an explicit closed‑form representation (7) once the
optimal KKT multipliers are known, and those multipliers are obtained by
solving the small linear systems indicated above.

Solution 8:
**Solution (KKT – a closed‑form expression)**  

Because the objective is a convex quadratic (assume \(M\succ0\)), the problem is a convex QP.  
Introduce multipliers  

* \(\lambda\ge 0\) for the return constraint \(\mu^{\top}\beta\ge\sigma\),  
* \(\nu\ge 0\) for the budget constraint \({\bf1}^{\top}\beta\le1\),  
* \(\eta\in\mathbb R^{p}_{+}\) for the non‑negativity constraints \(\beta_i\ge0\).

Write the constraints in the form  \(g_i(\beta)\le0\) :

\[
g_{0}(\beta)=\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta\le0,\qquad
g_{1}(\beta)={\bf1}^{\top}\beta-1\le0,\qquad
g_{i+1}(\beta)=-\beta_i\le0\;(i=1,\dots,p).
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\eta)
&=\beta^{\top}M\beta
+\lambda(\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta)
+\nu({\bf1}^{\top}\beta-1)
-\eta^{\top}\beta \\[2mm]
&=\beta^{\top}M\beta-\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}+\eta\bigr)^{\top}\beta
+\lambda\sigma-\nu .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 1. First‑order (stationarity) condition  

\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta}=2M\beta-(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}+\eta)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\,\beta=\frac12M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}+\eta\bigr)\,}. \tag{1}
\]

Since \(\eta_i\ge0\) and \(\eta_i\beta_i=0\) (complementary slackness), (1) can be rewritten as a **componentwise projection** onto the non‑negative orthant:

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta_i = \Bigl[\tfrac12\bigl(M^{-1}(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1})\bigr)_i\Bigr]_{+},
\qquad i=1,\dots,p,
\;}
\tag{2}
\]
where \([x]_{+}=\max\{0,x\}\).

---

### 2. Complementary‑slackness conditions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda\;(\sigma-\mu^{\top}\beta) &=0,\\
\nu\;({\bf1}^{\top}\beta-1) &=0,\\
\eta_i\,\beta_i &=0,\qquad i=1,\dots,p .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

Together with primal feasibility  

\[
\mu^{\top}\beta\ge\sigma,\qquad {\bf1}^{\top}\beta\le1,\qquad \beta\ge0 ,
\]

conditions (3) determine the multipliers \(\lambda,\nu\).

---

### 3. Determination of \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\)

*If both linear constraints are active* (the usual case in the portfolio‑selection interpretation), we have
\(\mu^{\top}\beta=\sigma\) and \({\bf1}^{\top}\beta=1\).  
Insert (2) without the positive‑part operator (i.e. assuming all components are strictly positive) and use (1):

\[
\beta=\frac12M^{-1}(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}) .
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{cases}
\mu^{\top}\beta = \dfrac12\,\mu^{\top}M^{-1}(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}) = \sigma,\\[2mm]
{\bf1}^{\top}\beta = \dfrac12\,{\bf1}^{\top}M^{-1}(\lambda\mu-\nu{\bf1}) = 1 .
\end{cases}
\]

These two linear equations give \(\lambda\) and \(\nu\):

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\mu^{\top}M^{-1}\mu & -\mu^{\top}M^{-1}{\bf1}\\[4pt]
{\bf1}^{\top}M^{-1}\mu & -{\bf1}^{\top}M^{-1}{\bf1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\lambda\\ \nu
\end{pmatrix}
=
2
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma\\ 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{4}
\]

If the solution of (4) yields \(\lambda<0\) or \(\nu<0\), the corresponding constraint is *not* binding; one repeats the calculation with the reduced active set (e.g. only the return constraint active, set \(\nu=0\); or only the budget constraint active, set \(\lambda=0\)).  

When an inequality is inactive its multiplier is zero, and the remaining active constraints are solved analogously.

---

### 4. Final expression for the optimal vector  

Collecting (2) and the rule for the multipliers we obtain the optimal solution of the original problem:

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{\star}= \Bigl[\,\frac12\,M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda^{\star}\,\mu-\nu^{\star}\,{\bf1}\bigr)\Bigr]_{+},
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

where the non‑negative scalars \(\lambda^{\star},\nu^{\star}\) satisfy the complementary‑slackness conditions (3) and the primal feasibility constraints.  

*If both constraints are binding* they are given explicitly by (4); otherwise the active‑set reduces to a single binding constraint, yielding \(\lambda^{\star}=0\) or \(\nu^{\star}=0\) and the corresponding one‑dimensional formula obtained from (1).

Equation (5) together with the rules for \(\lambda^{\star},\nu^{\star}\) provides the complete solution of the quadratic program.

Solution 9:
The problem is a **convex quadratic program** (the objective is a positive‑semidefinite quadratic form and all constraints are linear).  
Hence the optimal point \(\beta^{\star}\) is characterised by the Karush‑Kuhn‑Tucker (KKT) conditions.  

---

### 1.  Lagrangian  

Introduce the Lagrange multipliers  

* \(\lambda\ge 0\) for the inequality \(\mu^{\!T}\beta\ge\sigma\) (written as \(\sigma-\mu^{\!T}\beta\le 0\)),  
* \(\nu\ge 0\) for the inequality \(1^{T}\beta\le 1\), and  
* \(\alpha_i\ge 0\;(i=1,\dots ,p)\) for the non‑negativity constraints \(\beta_i\ge0\) (written as \(-\beta_i\le0\)).  

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal{L}(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\alpha)=\beta^{T}M\beta
      -\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)
      +\nu\bigl(1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)
      -\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_i\beta_i .
\]

---

### 2.  Stationarity  

\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\beta}=2M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\alpha=0,
\qquad\text{with }\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots ,\alpha_p)^{T}.
\tag{1}
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{\star}= \frac12\,M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1+\alpha\bigr)
\;}
\tag{2}
\]

(If \(M\) is singular, replace \(M^{-1}\) by the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse; the same KKT system still holds.)

---

### 3.  Complementary slackness  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda\bigl(\mu^{T}\beta-\sigma\bigr)&=0,\\[2pt]
\nu\bigl(1^{T}\beta-1\bigr)&=0,\\[2pt]
\alpha_i\beta_i&=0,\qquad i=1,\dots ,p .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

---

### 4.  Primal feasibility  

\[
\mu^{T}\beta\ge\sigma,\qquad
1^{T}\beta\le1,\qquad
\beta_i\ge0\;(i=1,\dots ,p).
\tag{4}
\]

---

### 5.  Dual feasibility  

\[
\lambda\ge0,\qquad \nu\ge0,\qquad \alpha_i\ge0\;(i=1,\dots ,p).
\tag{5}
\]

---

### 6.  Determination of the multipliers  

The optimal multipliers are obtained by solving the linear system that results from (1) together with the active‑set conditions in (3)–(5).  
In practice one proceeds as follows:

1. **Guess the active set**  
   \(\mathcal A=\{i:\beta_i=0\}\) (the indices for which the non‑negativity constraints are binding) and decide whether the equality
   \(\mu^{T}\beta=\sigma\) and/or \(1^{T}\beta=1\) is active.  

2. **Set the corresponding multipliers**  
   * if \(\mu^{T}\beta>\sigma\) then \(\lambda=0\); otherwise \(\lambda>0\),  
   * if \(1^{T}\beta<1\) then \(\nu=0\); otherwise \(\nu>0\),  
   * for each \(i\in\mathcal A\) set \(\alpha_i>0\); for \(i\notin\mathcal A\) set \(\alpha_i=0\).

3. **Solve the linear equations**  
   With the chosen active set, (1) reduces to a linear system for the unknowns
   \(\beta_{\mathcal F}\) (the free components) and the unknown multipliers
   \(\lambda,\nu\).  Solve this system; if the obtained solution satisfies all
   primal feasibility conditions, the guess was correct and the solution is
   optimal.  If not, modify the active set and repeat.

Because the problem is convex, the first feasible solution that satisfies the KKT conditions is the global minimiser.

---

### 7.  Closed‑form expression for the common special case  

If, at the optimum, **both inequality constraints are active** (i.e.  
\(\mu^{T}\beta^{\star}=\sigma\) and \(1^{T}\beta^{\star}=1\)) and none of the non‑negativity
constraints are binding (\(\beta^{\star}>0\)), then \(\alpha=0\) and (1) becomes  

\[
2M\beta^{\star}= \lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1 .
\]

Together with the two active constraints we obtain a linear system for
\(\lambda,\nu\) :

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu^{T}M^{-1}\mu & -\mu^{T}M^{-1}\mathbf 1\\[4pt]
-\mathbf 1^{T}M^{-1}\mu & \mathbf 1^{T}M^{-1}\mathbf 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda \\ \nu\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}2\sigma\\ 2\end{bmatrix},
\]

which gives \(\lambda,\nu\).  Substituting back into (2) yields  

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{\star}= \frac12\,M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1\bigr)
\;}
\qquad\text{with }\lambda,\nu\text{ obtained from the 2×2 system above.}
\]

If any component of this \(\beta^{\star}\) is negative, the corresponding index is added to the active set, the associated \(\alpha_i\) becomes positive, and the procedure is repeated until all \(\beta_i^{\star}\ge0\).

---

### 8.  Summary  

The optimal solution of the problem is the vector \(\beta^{\star}\) that satisfies the KKT conditions (1)–(5).  In compact form:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Find } \beta^{\star},\;\lambda\ge0,\;\nu\ge0,\;\alpha\ge0 \text{ such that}\\
&2M\beta^{\star}-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\alpha=0,\\
&\mu^{T}\beta^{\star}\ge\sigma,\;1^{T}\beta^{\star}\le1,\;\beta^{\star}\ge0,\\
&\lambda(\mu^{T}\beta^{\star}-\sigma)=0,\;
\nu(1^{T}\beta^{\star}-1)=0,\;
\alpha_i\beta^{\star}_i=0\;(i=1,\dots ,p).
\end{aligned}}

Solving this linear‑complementarity system (e.g., by an active‑set QP solver) yields the unique global minimiser because the objective is convex.

Solution 10:
Below is a complete, step‑by‑step derivation of the optimal solution.  
Throughout we assume that the symmetric matrix \(\mathbf M\) is **positive‑definite**
(\(\mathbf M\succ 0\)); then the objective \(\beta^{\!\top}\mathbf M\beta\) is strictly
convex and the quadratic programme has a unique minimiser.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Lagrangian and KKT conditions  

Introduce the (non‑negative) Lagrange multipliers  

\[
\lambda\ge 0 \qquad (\text{for } \mu^{\!\top}\beta\ge \sigma),\qquad   
\nu\ge 0 \qquad (\text{for } \mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta\le 1),\qquad   
\gamma_i\ge 0\;(i=1,\dots ,p)\; (\text{for } \beta_i\ge 0).
\]

The Lagrangian is  

\[
\mathcal L(\beta,\lambda,\nu,\gamma)
   =\beta^{\!\top}\!\mathbf M\beta
     +\lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\!\top}\beta\bigr)
     +\nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta-1\bigr)
     -\sum_{i=1}^{p}\gamma_i\beta_i .
\]

Taking the gradient with respect to \(\beta\) and setting it to zero gives  

\[
\boxed{ \; 2\mathbf M\beta-\lambda\mu+\nu\mathbf 1-\gamma =0 \;}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\beta = \frac12 \mathbf M^{-1}
        \bigl(\lambda\mu-\nu\mathbf 1+\gamma\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

The remaining KKT conditions are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\lambda\bigl(\sigma-\mu^{\!\top}\beta\bigr)=0, \qquad
  \nu\bigl(\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta-1\bigr)=0,\\[2mm]
&\gamma_i\beta_i =0,\qquad i=1,\dots ,p,\\[2mm]
&\sigma-\mu^{\!\top}\beta\le 0,\quad 
  \mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta-1\le 0,\quad 
  \beta_i\ge 0,\\
&\lambda,\nu,\gamma_i\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Structure of the solution  

From (1) we see that the optimal vector \(\beta^{\star}\) is a linear
combination of the two “direction’’ vectors \(\mathbf M^{-1}\mu\) and
\(\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1\), plus a non‑negative correction that
vanishes for every component that is strictly positive.  
Consequently the solution can be obtained by deciding **which**
constraints are active (i.e. hold with equality) and solving the linear
system that results from (1) together with the equalities.

Because the problem is convex, the optimal point lies on the boundary
of the feasible set; at least one of the three families of constraints
must be active:

* **(A)** \(\mu^{\!\top}\beta=\sigma\)  (the “mean’’ constraint);
* **(B)** \(\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta=1\) (the “budget’’ constraint);
* **(C)** \(\beta_i=0\) for some indices \(i\) (the non‑negativity constraints).

The algorithm is therefore:

1. **Start with the smallest active set, {A}.**  
   Set \(\gamma=\mathbf0\) and \(\nu=0\).  
   From (1) and the equality \(\mu^{\!\top}\beta=\sigma\) we obtain  

   \[
   \beta^{(A)}=
   \frac{\sigma}{\mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu}\,
   \mathbf M^{-1}\mu .
   \tag{3}
   \]

   If \(\beta^{(A)}\ge\mathbf0\) and \(\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta^{(A)}\le 1\)
   then (3) satisfies all constraints and is the optimal solution.

2. **If (3) violates a constraint, add the violated one to the active set.**  
   *If* \(\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta^{(A)}>1\) we make the budget constraint
   active as well (set \(\nu>0\)).  
   Solving (1) together with  

   \[
   \mu^{\!\top}\beta=\sigma,\qquad \mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta=1,
   \]

   gives  

   \[
   \beta^{(AB)}=
   \mathbf M^{-1}\Bigl(
        a\,\mu + b\,\mathbf 1
   \Bigr),\qquad
   \begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\end{bmatrix}
   =\frac{1}{\Delta}
   \begin{bmatrix}
      \mathbf 1^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1 & -\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu\\[2mm]
      -\mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1 & \mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu
   \end{bmatrix}
   \begin{bmatrix}\sigma\\ 1\end{bmatrix},
   \tag{4}
   \]

   where  

   \[
   \Delta=
   (\mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu)\,
   (\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1)
   -(\mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf 1)^2 >0 .
   \]

   If every component of \(\beta^{(AB)}\) is non‑negative, (4) is the
   optimal solution.

3. **If still some components are negative, set those components to zero**
   (they belong to set C) and resolve the reduced system.  
   Let \(I\subset\{1,\dots ,p\}\) be the index set of components that are
   forced to be zero.  Denote by \(\mathbf M_{II}\) the principal sub‑matrix
   of \(\mathbf M\) obtained by keeping only the rows and columns indexed
   by the complementary set \(J=\{1,\dots ,p\}\setminus I\).  Define the
   reduced vectors \(\mu_J,\mathbf 1_J\).  Solving (1) on the reduced
   coordinates with the possibly active constraints yields exactly the
   same formulas (3) or (4) with \(\mathbf M,\,\mu,\,\mathbf 1\) replaced
   by \(\mathbf M_{JJ},\,\mu_J,\,\mathbf 1_J\).  The resulting vector is
   then padded with zeros on the indices in \(I\).  
   This step is repeated until all components are non‑negative.

Because the feasible set is a polyhedron, the above “active‑set’’
procedure terminates after at most \(p\) iterations and returns the
unique global minimiser.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Compact closed‑form expression  

Collecting the three cases, the optimal solution can be written in the
single line  

\[
\boxed{\;
\beta^{\star}= \frac12\,
\mathbf M^{-1}\bigl(\lambda^{\star}\mu-\nu^{\star}\mathbf 1+\gamma^{\star}\bigr),
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

where the optimal multipliers \((\lambda^{\star},\nu^{\star},
\gamma^{\star})\) are the unique non‑negative solution of the linear
system obtained from the KKT equalities together with the complementary
slackness conditions (2).  In practice they are found by the active‑set
algorithm described above, which may be summarised as:

| active set | explicit formula for \(\beta^{\star}\) |
|------------|----------------------------------------|
| only \(\mu^{\!\top}\beta=\sigma\) | \(\displaystyle\beta^{\star}= \frac{\sigma}{\mu^{\!\top}\mathbf M^{-1}\mu}\,\mathbf M^{-1}\mu\) |
| \(\mu^{\!\top}\beta=\sigma,\; \mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta=1\) | \(\displaystyle\beta^{\star}= \mathbf M^{-1}\bigl(a\,\mu+b\,\mathbf 1\bigr)\) with \(a,b\) given by (4) |
| plus zero‑components on a set \(I\) | same formulas applied to the reduced sub‑problem on the
remaining indices |

The vector \(\beta^{\star}\) obtained from (5) (or equivalently from the
appropriate row of the table) is the unique minimiser of  

\[
\min_{\beta\ge0,\;\mu^{\!\top}\beta\ge\sigma,\;\mathbf 1^{\!\top}\beta\le1}
\beta^{\!\top}\mathbf M\beta .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Hence the solution of the optimisation problem is the point of the
feasible set that is closest to the origin in the norm induced by
\(\mathbf M\); it can be expressed explicitly as (5) with the optimal
multipliers obtained from the KKT/active‑set conditions described
above.**

Let  

* \(A\) = a person who pays with a \(5\,000\)‑Rp note (he gives the seller a 5 000 note),  
* \(B\) = a person who pays with a \(10\,000\)‑Rp note (the seller must give a 5 000 change).

There are  

\[
7\;A\text{'s},\qquad 5\;B\text{'s},
\]

and the 12 people stand in a random order.  
The seller starts with one \(5\,000\)‑Rp note.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Translating to a walk

After the first \(i\) customers let  

\[
a_i=\#\text{ of }A\text{ among the first }i,\qquad 
b_i=\#\text{ of }B\text{ among the first }i .
\]

The number of \(5\,000\) notes the seller has after those \(i\) customers is  

\[
f_i = 1 + a_i - b_i .
\]

The seller can give change iff he never runs out of 5 000‑notes, i.e.  

\[
f_i\ge 0\quad\text{for every }i=0,1,\dots ,12 .
\]

Thus we need  

\[
b_i \le a_i+1\qquad\text{for every prefix }i .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Adding a dummy \(A\)

Condition (1) can be turned into the ordinary ballot condition by inserting one
*dummy* \(A\) at the very beginning – this dummy represents the initial
\(5\,000\) note.  
Now we have  

\[
8\;A\text{'s} \;(7\text{ real}+1\text{ dummy})\,,\qquad 5\;B\text{'s}.
\]

For the combined string of length \(13\) we require

\[
\#A\text{ in every prefix } \ge \#B\text{ in that prefix}.
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Counting sequences that satisfy (2)

The number of strings with \(p\) \(A\)’s and \(q\) \(B\)’s that obey (2) is given by the
ballot theorem:

\[
N(p,q)=\frac{p-q+1}{p+1}\binom{p+q}{q}.
\]

Here \(p=8,\;q=5\). Hence

\[
N(8,5)=\frac{8-5+1}{8+1}\binom{13}{5}
     =\frac{4}{9}\times1287
     =572 .
\]

Each such string begins with the dummy \(A\); removing that first symbol
produces a unique ordering of the **12 real customers** that allows the seller to give change.
Thus there are \(572\) successful orders.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Total possible orders

The only thing that matters is which positions are occupied by the five
\(B\)-customers.  The number of all possible orders is

\[
\binom{12}{5}=792 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Probability

\[
\displaystyle
\Pr(\text{seller never runs out of change})
   =\frac{572}{792}
   =\frac{13}{18}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\dfrac{13}{18}}
\]

Solution 1:
The seller starts with one 5 000‑Rp note.  
Let  

* \(a_k\) = number of 5 000‑Rp customers served after the first \(k\) people,  
* \(b_k\) = number of 10 000‑Rp customers served after the first \(k\) people.

When a 5 000‑Rp customer arrives the seller gains a 5 000 note (\(+1\)), and when a 10 000‑Rp customer arrives the seller must give a 5 000‑Rp change (\(-1\)).  
The seller can serve everyone iff the cash on hand never becomes negative:

\[
1 + a_k - b_k \ge 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad a_k \ge b_k-1\quad\text{for all }k.
\]

Thus, in every prefix of the queue the number of 5 000‑Rp customers must be at least the number of 10 000‑Rp customers minus one.

We have 7 customers with 5 000‑Rp notes (\(a=7\)) and 5 customers with 10 000‑Rp notes (\(b=5\)).  
The number of permutations of these 12 customers satisfying \(a_k\ge b_k-1\) is given by the ballot‑problem formula with an initial surplus of one:

\[
\#\text{valid orderings}= \frac{a+1-b}{a+1}\binom{a+b}{b}
    = \frac{7+1-5}{7+1}\binom{12}{5}
    = \frac{3}{8}\times 792 = 297 .
\]

The total number of possible orderings is \(\displaystyle\binom{12}{5}=792\).

Hence  

\[
\Pr(\text{enough change}) = \frac{297}{792}= \frac{3}{8}=0.375 .
\]

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{3}{8}}
\]

Solution 2:
**Step‑by‑step reasoning**

1. **Identify the two types of customers**
   * 7 customers have a 5,000‑Rp note (they need no change). Call them **B**.
   * 5 customers have a 10,000‑Rp note (they need 5,000 Rp change). Call them **A**.

2. **Initial condition**
   * The seller starts with one 5,000‑Rp note.  
   * This can be thought of as an extra “B” that is already available before any customer is served.

3. **Re‑formulate the problem**
   * After adding the initial note, we have **8 B’s** (7 real + 1 initial) and **5 A’s**.
   * The seller can serve everyone iff, at every point in the line, the number of A‑customers that have appeared is **never larger** than the number of B‑customers that have appeared (including the initial one).  
   * In other words, in the sequence of 13 symbols (8 B, 5 A) we must never have more A’s than B’s in any prefix.

4. **Use the ballot (Catalan) count**
   * For \(a\) A’s and \(b\) B’s with \(a<b\), the number of admissible sequences where A never exceeds B is  

\[
N = \frac{b+1-a}{\,b+1\,}\binom{a+b}{a}.
\]

   * Here \(a=5,\; b=8\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{8+1-5}{9}\binom{13}{5}
   = \frac{4}{9}\times 1287
   = 572 .
\end{aligned}
\]

5. **Total possible orders**
   * All possible orders of the 12 real customers (ignoring the initial note) are  

\[
\binom{12}{5}=1287 .
\]

6. **Probability**
   * The required probability is the ratio of admissible orders to all orders:

\[
P = \frac{572}{1287}= \frac{4}{9}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{4}{9}}
\]

Solution 3:
Let  

* a customer who pays with a **5 000‑Rp** note be denoted by \(A\) (he gives the seller a 5 000‑Rp note, no change is needed);  
* a customer who pays with a **10 000‑Rp** note be denoted by \(B\) (the seller must give him a 5 000‑Rp note as change).

The seller begins the day with **one** 5 000‑Rp note.  
If after serving the first \(i\) customers we denote  

\[
a_i=\#\{A\text{'s among the first }i\},\qquad 
b_i=\#\{B\text{'s among the first }i\},
\]

then his stock of 5 000‑Rp notes is  

\[
\text{stock}_i = 1 + a_i - b_i .
\]

The seller can continue serving only while \(\text{stock}_i\ge 0\); i.e.

\[
1+a_i-b_i\ge 0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad a_i\ge b_i-1\quad\text{for every }i.
\]

Thus we must count the permutations of the 12 customers (5 of type \(B\) and 7 of type \(A\)) that satisfy this “ballot” condition.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Transform to a lattice‑path problem
Give each \(A\) an “up‑step’’ \((+1)\) and each \(B\) a “down‑step’’ \((-1)\).  
Start at height \(1\) (the initial 5 000‑Rp note).  
The condition above is exactly that the path never goes below height \(0\).

If we prepend the initial up‑step to the sequence, we obtain a path that
starts at height \(0\) and has  

* total up‑steps \(p = 7+1 = 8\),  
* total down‑steps \(q = 5\),

and never falls below the horizontal axis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Number of admissible sequences (ballot numbers)

For \(p\ge q\) the number of such paths is the ballot number  

\[
N(p,q)=\frac{p-q+1}{p+1}\binom{p+q}{q}.
\]

Here \(p=8,\;q=5\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
N(8,5)&=\frac{8-5+1}{8+1}\binom{13}{5}
      =\frac{4}{9}\times 1287
      =572 .
\end{aligned}
\]

So there are **572** distinct type‑orders that allow the seller to give change.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Total possible type‑orders

Only the positions of the five \(B\)’s matter; the remaining seven are \(A\)’s.  
The total number of possible type‑orders is

\[
\binom{12}{5}=792 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Probability

\[
\displaystyle 
P=\frac{\text{good orders}}{\text{all orders}}
   =\frac{572}{792}
   =\frac{13}{18}\approx 0.7222 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{13}{18}}
\] 

Thus, when the 12 people line up in a random order, the ticket seller will have enough change for everyone with probability \(13/18\) (about \(72.2\%\)).

Solution 4:
Let  

* \(7\) people have a \(5{,}000\)‑Rp note (they need no change).  
* \(5\) people have a \(10{,}000\)‑Rp note (they need a \(5{,}000\)‑Rp change).  

Denote by  

* \(X_k\) = number of 5 000‑Rp customers served after the first \(k\) people,  
* \(Y_k\) = number of 10 000‑Rp customers served after the first \(k\) people.

The seller begins with one \(5{,}000\)‑Rp note.  
After the first \(k\) customers he will have  

\[
\text{change}=1+X_k-Y_k
\]

five‑thousand‑rupiah notes.  
He can give change to the next customer iff this quantity is non‑negative, i.e.

\[
1+X_k-Y_k\ge 0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Y_k\le X_k+1 .
\]

Thus in the whole ordering we must never have more \(10{,}000\)‑Rp customers served than the number of \(5{,}000\)‑Rp customers already served plus one.

---

### Transform to a classic ballot problem  

Imagine that the seller initially possessed an “extra” 5 000‑Rp customer.  
Add this fictitious customer to the list of \(5{,}000\)‑Rp payers.  

Now we have  

* \(8\) “\(5{,}000\)” customers (the original 7 plus the extra one),  
* \(5\) “\(10{,}000\)” customers,

and the condition becomes simply  

\[
\text{at every point } \; X'_k \ge Y_k ,
\]

i.e. the number of \(5{,}000\) customers never falls behind the number of \(10{,}000\) customers.

This is exactly the ballot problem with ties allowed.  
For \(A\) votes of type A and \(B\) votes of type B \((A\ge B)\), the probability that in a random permutation the cumulative votes of A are never fewer than those of B is  

\[
\frac{A-B+1}{A+1}.
\]

Here \(A=8\) and \(B=5\), so the required probability is  

\[
\frac{8-5+1}{8+1}= \frac{4}{9}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{4}{9}}
\]

Solution 5:
Each customer either pays with a 5 000‑Rp note (exact payment) or with a 10 000‑Rp note (needs 5 000‑Rp change).  
Let  

* \(A\): a customer with a 5 000‑Rp note (there are 7 of them),  
* \(B\): a customer with a 10 000‑Rp note (there are 5 of them).

The order of the 12 customers is a random permutation of the 7 \(A\)’s and 5 \(B\)’s.  
If the seller begins with **no change**, then after the first \(k\) customers the seller’s stock of 5 000‑Rp notes equals  

\[
\#A\;(k)-\#B\;(k).
\]

He can serve the next customer only when this quantity is non‑negative.  
Thus a sequence of customers is acceptable iff for **every** prefix of the sequence  

\[
\#A\;(k)\;\ge\;\#B\;(k).
\]

So we must count the permutations of 7 \(A\)’s and 5 \(B\)’s whose prefixes never have more \(B\)’s than \(A\)’s.

---

### Ballot theorem

For \(p\) votes of type \(A\) and \(q\) votes of type \(B\) with \(p\ge q\), the number of sequences in which the count of \(A\) never falls below that of \(B\) is  

\[
\frac{p-q+1}{p+1}\binom{p+q}{q}.
\]

Here \(p=7\) and \(q=5\). Hence

\[
\text{favourable sequences}
 =\frac{7-5+1}{7+1}\binom{12}{5}
 =\frac{3}{8}\times 792
 =297 .
\]

The total number of possible orders of the 12 customers is simply  

\[
\binom{12}{5}=792 .
\]

---

### Probability

\[
\Pr(\text{seller can give change to everyone})
 =\frac{297}{792}
 =\frac{3}{8}=0.375 .
\]

\[
\boxed{\dfrac{3}{8}}
