Solution 0:
\[
|G|=350=2\cdot5^{2}\cdot 7 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Sylow subgroups  

* **Sylow \(7\)-subgroup.**  
  \(\displaystyle n_{7}\mid 2\cdot5^{2}=50\) and \(n_{7}\equiv1\pmod 7\).  
  The only divisor of \(50\) congruent to \(1\bmod 7\) is \(n_{7}=1\).  
  Hence the Sylow‑\(7\) subgroup \(P_{7}\) (order \(7\)) is unique and therefore **normal**.

* **Sylow \(5\)-subgroup.**  
  \(\displaystyle n_{5}\mid 2\cdot7=14\) and \(n_{5}\equiv1\pmod5\).  
  The only divisor of \(14\) satisfying this is \(n_{5}=1\).  
  So the Sylow‑\(5\) subgroup \(P_{5}\) (order \(5^{2}=25\)) is also **normal**.

* **Sylow \(2\)-subgroup.**  
  \(\displaystyle n_{2}\mid 5^{2}\cdot7=175,\; n_{2}\equiv1\pmod2\).  
  Any odd divisor of \(175\) (\(1,5,7,25,35,175\)) can occur; we only need that a Sylow \(2\)-subgroup
  \(P_{2}\) of order \(2\) exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Structure of \(G\)

Because the Hall‑subgroup \(P_{5}P_{7}\) (order \(25\cdot7=175\)) is normal, we have  

\[
G = (P_{5}\times P_{7})\rtimes P_{2},
\qquad |P_{5}\times P_{7}|=175,\;|P_{2}|=2 .
\]

A group of order \(p^{2}\;(p\) prime) is abelian, so \(P_{5}\) is abelian; its subgroups are of
orders \(1,5,25\).  \(P_{7}\) is cyclic of order \(7\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Subgroups of the required orders  

#### (a) Order \(10\)  

Pick any element \(x\in P_{5}\) of order \(5\) (exists by Cauchy).  
Take any element \(t\in P_{2}\) of order \(2\).  
Since \(P_{5}\) is normal, \(t\,x\,t^{-1}\in P_{5}\).  
The induced automorphism of \(P_{5}\) by \(t\) has order dividing \(2\);
hence \(t x t^{-1}=x\) or \(x^{-1}\).  

Consequently \(\langle t,x\rangle\) is a group of order

\[
|\langle t,x\rangle|=\frac{|t|\cdot|x|}{|t\cap\langle x\rangle|}=2\cdot5=10 .
\]

Thus **every group of order \(350\) has a subgroup of order \(10\)** (it is either
\(C_{10}\) or the dihedral group \(D_{10}\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### (b) Order \(70\)

Choose a subgroup \(K\le P_{5}\) of order \(5\) (as above) that is *fixed* by the
automorphism induced by an element of \(P_{2}\).  
Because the involution on the abelian group \(P_{5}\) either fixes every element
or sends each to its inverse, such a \(K\) always exists (the unique subgroup
of order \(5\) in the cyclic case, or a \(1\)-dimensional subspace in the
\(C_{5}\times C_{5}\) case).

Now consider

\[
H = K\,P_{7}\le P_{5}\times P_{7},\qquad |H|=5\cdot7=35 .
\]

\(H\) is normal in the Hall‑subgroup \(P_{5}\times P_{7}\); being normalized by
\(t\in P_{2}\) (by the choice of \(K\)), the product

\[
\langle t\rangle H
\]

is a subgroup of \(G\) of order  

\[
|\,\langle t\rangle H| = | \langle t\rangle|\,|H| = 2\cdot35 = 70 .
\]

Hence **every group of order \(350\) contains a subgroup of order \(70\)**.

### 4.  All possible subgroup orders  

Since the only divisors of \(350\) are  

\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;7,\;10,\;14,\;25,\;35,\;50,\;70,\;175,\;350,
\]

and we have exhibited subgroups of each of these sizes (for the mixed
orders we use the normal Sylow‑\(5\) and Sylow‑\(7\) subgroups together with a
Sylow‑\(2\) subgroup as above), every divisor occurs as the order of a
subgroup of \(G\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\text{A group of order }350\text{ has subgroups of every divisor, in particular of orders }10\text{ and }70.}
\]

Equivalently, the set of subgroup orders is  

\[
\boxed{\{1,2,5,7,10,14,25,35,50,70,175,350\}} .
\]

Let  

\[
|G| = 350 = 2\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7 .
\]

Write the Sylow numbers  

\[
n_{7}\mid 2\cdot 5^{2}=50,\qquad n_{7}\equiv 1\pmod 7,
\]  

\[
n_{5}\mid 2\cdot 7 = 14,\qquad n_{5}\equiv 1\pmod 5 .
\]

The only divisors of \(50\) that are \(\equiv 1\pmod 7\) are \(1\); hence  

\[
n_{7}=1 .
\]

Thus the Sylow‑\(7\) subgroup \(P_{7}\) (order \(7\)) is **normal** in \(G\).

Similarly, the only divisor of \(14\) that is \(\equiv 1\pmod 5\) is \(1\); therefore  

\[
n_{5}=1 ,
\]

so the Sylow‑\(5\) subgroup \(P_{5}\) (order \(25\)) is also normal in \(G\).

Consequences  

* \(P_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) are normal, so their product  

\[
N = P_{5}P_{7}\cong P_{5}\times P_{7}
\]

is a normal subgroup of order  

\[
|N| = 25\cdot 7 = 175 .
\]

* Any group of order \(25\) is abelian, hence \(P_{5}\) contains a unique subgroup of order \(5\); denote it by \(Q_{5}\) (\(|Q_{5}|=5\)).

* Let \(P_{2}\) be a Sylow‑\(2\) subgroup of \(G\) (\(|P_{2}|=2\)).  Its existence is guaranteed by Sylow’s theorem; we do not need it to be normal.

---

### Subgroup of order \(70 = 2\cdot5\cdot7\)

Consider  

\[
H_{70}= P_{2}\, Q_{5}\, P_{7}.
\]

Because \(P_{7}\) and \(Q_{5}\) are normal in \(G\), they commute with each other and with the elements of \(P_{2}\).  Hence  

\[
|H_{70}| = |P_{2}|\;|Q_{5}|\;|P_{7}| = 2\cdot5\cdot7 = 70 .
\]

Thus \(G\) possesses a subgroup of order \(70\).

---

### Subgroup of order \(10 = 2\cdot5\)

Similarly,  

\[
H_{10}= P_{2}\, Q_{5},
\]

has  

\[
|H_{10}| = 2\cdot5 = 10 .
\]

Hence a subgroup of order \(10\) also exists.

---

Because \(G\) has order \(p^{a}q^{b}\) (with \(p,q\) primes), Burnside’s theorem tells us that **every** group of order \(350\) is solvable; Hall’s theorem for solvable groups guarantees the existence of Hall subgroups of any order dividing \(350\) that is the product of some of its prime‑power factors.  The orders \(70\) and \(10\) satisfy this condition, confirming the conclusions above.

\[
\boxed{\text{A group } G\text{ of order }350\text{ has subgroups of orders }70\text{ and }10.}
\]

Because the normal subgroup \(N\) (order \(25\)) contains a subgroup
\(H_{5}\) of order \(5\) (any group of order \(25\) has such a subgroup),
the product  

\[
H_{35}=H_{5}\,P_{7}
\]

has order \(|H_{5}|\cdot|P_{7}| = 5\cdot 7 = 35\) (the two factors intersect
trivially).  
Since \(\operatorname{Aut}(C_{5})\cong C_{4}\) and \(7\nmid 4\), the only possible
semidirect product of \(C_{5}\) by \(C_{7}\) is the direct product;
hence \(H_{35}\cong C_{35}\) is cyclic.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Subgroup of order \(70 = 2\cdot 5\cdot 7\)

Now combine the cyclic subgroup \(H_{35}\) with a Sylow‑2 subgroup
\(P_{2}\) of order \(2\).  
Because \(\gcd(2,35)=1\), the product  

\[
H_{70}=H_{35}\,P_{2}
\]

has order \(35\cdot 2 = 70\).  
Thus \(G\) contains a subgroup of order \(70\) (it may be cyclic
\(C_{70}\) or a non‑trivial semidirect product, but its existence is
guaranteed).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Subgroup of order \(10 = 2\cdot 5\)

Inside the normal Sylow‑5 subgroup \(N\) choose a subgroup \(H_{5}\) of
order \(5\).  The product with a Sylow‑2 subgroup gives  

\[
H_{10}=H_{5}\,P_{2},
\qquad |H_{10}| = 5\cdot 2 = 10 .
\]

Again the two factors intersect trivially, so a subgroup of order \(10\)
exists (it is either cyclic \(C_{10}\) or the dihedral group
\(D_{5}\)).

### 5.  Hall’s theorem (alternative viewpoint)

A group whose order is \(p^{a}q^{b}r^{c}\) with three primes \(p,q,r\)
is solvable (Burnside’s \(p^{a}q^{b}\) theorem).  
For any set of primes \(\pi\) there exists a Hall \(\pi\)-subgroup.
Taking \(\pi=\{2,5,7\}\) gives a subgroup of order \(70\);
taking \(\pi=\{2,5\}\) gives a subgroup of order \(10\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\text{Every group of order }350\text{ possesses subgroups of orders }70\text{ and }10.}
\]

\[

\[

We now show that each of these divisors actually occurs as the order of a subgroup of **any** group

The only non‑trivial facts needed are Sylow’s theorems and the fact that a group of order \(p^{2}\) has a

---

### 1.  Sylow subgroups

* \(n_{5}\equiv1\pmod5,\; n_{5}\mid 14\) ⇒ \(n_{5}=1\).
  Hence the Sylow‑5 subgroup \(P\) of order \(25\) is **normal**.

* \(n_{7}\equiv1\pmod7,\; n_{7}\mid 50\) ⇒ \(n_{7}=1\) or \(50\).  
  In any case a Sylow‑7 subgroup \(Q\) of order \(7\) exists.

* \(n_{2}\equiv1\pmod2,\; n_{2}\mid175\) ⇒ \(n_{2}\) is odd; a Sylow‑2 subgroup \(R\) of order \(2\) exists.

Thus groups of orders \(25,7,2\) are always present.

---

### 2.  Subgroups of order \(5\)

Since \(P\cong\mathbb{Z}_{5^{2}}\) or \(\mathbb{Z}_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{5}\), it contains a subgroup
\(A\) of order \(5\).  
\(A\) is characteristic in \(P\) and \(P\trianglelefteq G\); therefore \(A\trianglelefteq G\).

---

### 3.  Constructing the required orders  

* **Order \(10=2\cdot5\).**  
  \(A\) (order 5) is normal and \(R\) (order 2) is any Sylow‑2 subgroup.
  The product \(AR\) is a subgroup; because \(A\cap R=1\),

  \[
  |AR|=\frac{|A||R|}{|A\cap R|}=5\cdot2=10 .
  \]

* **Order \(14=2\cdot7\).**  
  By Hall’s theorem for solvable groups (every group of order \(350\) is solvable), there exists a
  Hall \(\{2,7\}\)-subgroup; denote it by \(H\).  Then \(|H|=14\).

* **Order \(35=5\cdot7\).**  
  The product \(AQ\) (with \(Q\) a Sylow‑7 subgroup) is a subgroup of order \(5\cdot7=35\).

* **Order \(70=2\cdot5\cdot7\).**  
  Take the Hall \(\{2,7\}\)-subgroup \(H\) of order \(14\) and the normal subgroup \(A\) of order \(5\).
  Since \(A\trianglelefteq G\),

  \[
  AH\le G,\qquad |AH|=\frac{|A||H|}{|A\cap H|}=5\cdot 14=70 .
  \]

* **Order \(50=2\cdot5^{2}\).**  
  \(PR\) (normal \(P\) of order \(25\) times a Sylow‑2) has order \(25\cdot2=50\).

* **Order \(175=5^{2}\cdot7\).**  
  \(PQ\) (normal \(P\) of order \(25\) times a Sylow‑7) has order \(25\cdot7=175\).

Together with the trivial subgroup and \(G\) itself we have found a subgroup for each divisor of
\(350\).

---

### 4.  Conclusion  

Every divisor of \(350\) occurs as the order of a subgroup of an arbitrary group \(G\) of order
\(350\). In particular, the construction above guarantees the existence of subgroups of the
requested orders

\[
\boxed{\text{order }10\ \text{and order }70}
\]

(and, indeed, subgroups of all the other divisors
\(1,2,5,7,14,25,35,50,175,350\)).  Hence the set of possible subgroup orders is

\[
\boxed{\{1,2,5,7,10,14,25,35,50,70,175,350\}} .
\]

\[
P_{2}\in \operatorname{Syl}_{2}(G),\qquad  
P_{5}\in \operatorname{Syl}_{5}(G),\qquad  
P_{7}\in \operatorname{Syl}_{7}(G)
\]

for Sylow subgroups of orders \(2,25\) and \(7\) respectively.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The Sylow–7 and Sylow‑5 subgroups are normal  

\[
n_{7}\equiv 1\pmod 7,\qquad n_{7}\mid 2\cdot5^{2}=50
\]

The only divisor of \(50\) that is \( \equiv 1\pmod 7\) is \(1\); hence  
\(n_{7}=1\) and \(P_{7}\lhd G\).

\[
n_{5}\equiv 1\pmod 5,\qquad n_{5}\mid 2\cdot7 =14
\]

The only divisor of \(14\) congruent to \(1\) mod \(5\) is \(1\); thus  
\(n_{5}=1\) and \(P_{5}\lhd G\).

Consequently  

\[
N:=P_{5}P_{7}\cong P_{5}\times P_{7}
\]

is a **normal** subgroup of order \(25\cdot7=175\).  
Both \(P_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) are characteristic in \(N\); therefore the
Sylow‑2 subgroup \(P_{2}\) normalises each of them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Subgroups of order \(35\) and \(70\)

Because \(P_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) are normal and have coprime orders,
their product is a direct product, which is cyclic:

\[
C_{35}=P_{5}P_{7}\cong C_{5}\times C_{7}\cong C_{35},
\qquad |C_{35}|=35 .
\]

\(C_{35}\) is normal in \(G\).  Multiplying it by the (non‑trivial)
Sylow‑2 subgroup gives

\[
\langle C_{35},P_{2}\rangle = C_{35}\rtimes P_{2},
\qquad |\,C_{35}\rtimes P_{2}\,| = 35\cdot2 = 70 .
\]

Hence **\(G\) always contains a subgroup of order \(70\)** (it is either
cyclic \(C_{70}\) or dihedral \(D_{35}\), depending on whether the
involution acts trivially or by inversion on \(C_{35}\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Subgroups of order \(10\)

Inside the normal Sylow‑5 subgroup \(P_{5}\) there are subgroups of order
\(5\) (Cauchy’s theorem).  Choose one and call it \(C_{5}\le P_{5}\).
Since \(P_{5}\) is normal, \(P_{2}\) normalises \(C_{5}\); therefore

\[
\langle C_{5},P_{2}\rangle = C_{5}\rtimes P_{2},
\qquad |\,C_{5}\rtimes P_{2}\,| = 5\cdot2 = 10 .
\]

Thus **\(G\) always contains a subgroup of order \(10\)** (again either
the cyclic group \(C_{10}\) or the dihedral group \(D_{5}\)).

### 4.  In fact, every divisor of \(350\) occurs

Using the normal subgroups \(P_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) together with the

\[
1,2,5,7,10,14,25,35,50,70,175,350 .

\[

\[
|G| = 350 = 2\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7 .

---

### 1.  Sylow sub‑groups  

* **\(5\)-Sylow.**  
  The number \(n_{5}\) of Sylow‑\(5\) subgroups satisfies  

  \[
  n_{5}\equiv 1\pmod 5,\qquad n_{5}\mid 2\cdot7 =14 .
  \]

  The only possibility is \(n_{5}=1\).  
  Hence there is a **unique normal** subgroup  

  \[
  P_{5}\;(\,|P_{5}|=5^{2}=25\,).
  \]

* **\(7\)-Sylow.**  
  \(n_{7}\equiv 1\pmod 7,\; n_{7}\mid 2\cdot5^{2}=50\).  
  Again the only divisor of 50 congruent to \(1\) modulo \(7\) is \(1\); thus  

  \[
  P_{7}\;(\,|P_{7}|=7\,)
  \]

  is normal.

* **\(2\)-Sylow.**  
  Let \(P_{2}\) be a Sylow‑\(2\) subgroup, \(|P_{2}|=2\).  
  The number of such subgroups can be \(1,5,7,25,35\) or \(175\); we do **not** need its exact value.

---

### 2.  Subgroups of orders \(70\) and \(10\)

Because \(P_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) are normal, any subgroup of them is also normal in \(G\).

* Choose a subgroup \(H_{5}\le P_{5}\) of order \(5\) (such a subgroup exists because a group of order \(25\) always has subgroups of order \(5\)).  
  Then \(H_{5}\) and \(P_{7}\) are normal, intersect trivially, and have coprime orders.

* The product  

  \[
  H_{5}P_{7}P_{2}\;=\; \{h_5p_7p_2\mid h_5\in H_{5},\,p_7\in P_{7},\,p_2\in P_{2}\}
  \]

  is a subgroup of \(G\).  
  Its order is the product of the three coprime orders:

  \[
  |H_{5}P_{7}P_{2}|=5\cdot7\cdot2=70 .
  \]

  Thus **\(G\) always contains a subgroup of order \(70\).**

* Similarly, the product  

  \[
  H_{5}P_{2}
  \]

  has order  

  \[
  |H_{5}P_{2}| = 5\cdot 2 = 10 ,
  \]

  giving a subgroup of order \(10\).

Hence a group of order \(350\) must contain subgroups of both orders \(70\) and \(10\).

---

### 3.  All possible subgroup orders  

Since every subgroup order must divide \(|G|=350\) (Lagrange) and we have shown that the Sylow‑\(5\) and Sylow‑\(7\) subgroups are normal, every divisor of \(350\) that can be written as a product of a divisor of \(25\), a divisor of \(7\) and optionally the factor \(2\) actually occurs.  
Consequently the list of subgroup orders that are guaranteed to exist in **any** group of order \(350\) is  

\[
\boxed{1,\;2,\;5,\;7,\;10,\;14,\;25,\;35,\;50,\;70,\;175,\;350 } .
\]

In particular, the orders asked for are present:

\[
\boxed{70\text{ and }10}.
\]

Solution 6:
Let  

\[
|G| = 350 = 2\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7 .
\]

Denote by \(P_{5}\) a Sylow \(5\)-subgroup of \(G\).  
By the Sylow theorems  

\[
n_{5}\equiv 1\pmod 5,\qquad n_{5}\mid 2\cdot 7 =14 ,
\]

so the only possibility is  

\[
n_{5}=1 .
\]

Hence **the Sylow‑\(5\) subgroup \(P_{5}\) is unique and therefore normal** in \(G\); \(|P_{5}|=5^{2}=25\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Subgroups of order \(10 = 2\cdot 5\)

* Take any Sylow‑\(2\) subgroup \(P_{2}\) of \(G\); \(|P_{2}|=2\).
* Inside the normal \(P_{5}\) choose a subgroup \(K\) of order \(5\) (every group of order \(25\) has subgroups of order \(5\)).

Because \(P_{2}\cap K = \{e\}\) and \(P_{2}\) normalises \(K\) ( \(K\le P_{5}\trianglelefteq G\) ), the product  

\[
H = P_{2}K
\]

is a subgroup of \(G\). Its order is

\[
|H| = |P_{2}|\;|K| = 2\cdot 5 = 10 .
\]

Thus **every group of order \(350\) possesses a subgroup of order \(10\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Subgroups of order \(70 = 2\cdot 5\cdot 7\)

Write  

\[
70 = 5\cdot 14 .
\]

If a subgroup of order \(70\) existed, it would contain a subgroup of order \(5\) and a subgroup of order \(14\) that intersect trivially.  
Consider the quotient by the normal Sylow‑\(5\) subgroup:

\[
\overline{G}=G/P_{5}, \qquad |\overline{G}| = \frac{350}{25}=14 .
\]

Every group of order \(14\) is a semidirect product \(C_{7}\rtimes C_{2}\); it **does have** a subgroup of order \(14\) (the whole group) but **does not contain a proper subgroup of order \(14\) that lifts to a subgroup of \(G\) of order \(70\)**, because any subgroup of \(\overline{G}\) that lifts must contain the whole image of \(P_{5}\) (which has order \(25\)).  

Consequently a subgroup of order \(70\) would correspond to a subgroup of \(\overline{G}\) of order \(14\) together with a *proper* subgroup of \(P_{5}\) of order \(5\).  
The difficulty is that a subgroup of order \(5\) of the normal \(P_{5}\) need **not** be normal in \(G\); without normality we cannot guarantee that the product of that order‑\(5\) subgroup with the pre‑image of a subgroup of \(\overline{G}\) is a subgroup of \(G\).

Indeed, there are groups of order \(350\) (for instance a non‑abelian semidirect product
\( (C_{5}\times C_{5})\rtimes (C_{7}\rtimes C_{2})\)) in which **no** subgroup of order \(70\) exists.  
Thus the existence of a subgroup of order \(70\) is **not forced** by the order \(350\) alone; it may or may not occur depending on the particular group structure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Result

*Every group of order \(350\) certainly has a subgroup of order \(10\).  
A subgroup of order \(70\) is **not guaranteed**; some groups of order \(350\) have such a subgroup, others do not.*

\[
\boxed{\text{Order }10\text{ – always exists; order }70\text{ – not guaranteed.}}
\]

\langle h\rangle L \le G,\qquad

### 4.  All possible orders

Every divisor of \(350\),

\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;7,\;10,\;14,\;25,\;35,\;50,\;70,\;175,\;350,

### 2.  Solvability of a group of order \(350\)

Burnside’s \(p^{a}q^{b}\) theorem says that any finite group whose order is the product of powers of at most two distinct primes is solvable.

\[
350 = 2\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7 = (2\cdot5^{2})\cdot 7,

\(G\) is a solvable group.

### 3.  Hall subgroups in solvable groups  

A **Hall \(\pi\)-subgroup** of a finite group is a subgroup whose order is the product of the primes in a set \(\pi\) (each taken to the first power) and whose index is relatively prime to that order.  

A theorem of Hall (proved for solvable groups) states:

> *If \(G\) is solvable, then for every set \(\pi\) of primes dividing \(|G|\) there exists a Hall \(\pi\)-subgroup of \(G\). Moreover any two Hall \(\pi\)-subgroups are conjugate.*

Hence, for each choice of a subset of \(\{2,5,7\}\) we obtain a subgroup whose order is the product of the primes in that subset.

---

### 4.  Applying Hall’s theorem to the required orders  

* **Order \(70\):** take \(\pi=\{2,5,7\}\).  
  The corresponding Hall \(\pi\)-subgroup has order  

  \[
  2\cdot5\cdot7 = 70 .
  \]

* **Order \(10\):** take \(\pi=\{2,5\}\).  
  The corresponding Hall \(\pi\)-subgroup has order  

  \[
  2\cdot5 = 10 .
  \]

Thus a solvable group of order \(350\) must contain subgroups of both orders \(70\) and \(10\).

---

Every group \(G\) with \(|G|=350\) possesses subgroups of order \(70\) and of order \(10\).  

\[
\boxed{\text{A group of order }350\text{ always has subgroups of orders }70\text{ and }10.}

We need a closed form for  

\[
S_r=\sum_{s=0}^{r}(-1)^s\,(r-s+1)\,C_s,
\qquad 0\le r\le n .

---

### 1.  Split the factor \(r-s+1\)

\[
r-s+1=(r+1)-s,
\]

\[
S_r=(r+1)\sum_{s=0}^{r}(-1)^s\binom{n}{s}
      \;-\;
      \sum_{s=0}^{r}s(-1)^s\binom{n}{s}
      \equiv (r+1)A_r-B_r .

### 2.  The alternating partial sum \(A_r\)

A well‑known identity for alternating binomial sums is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{k=0}^{m}(-1)^k\binom{N}{k}=(-1)^m\binom{N-1}{m}}
\qquad (N\ge 1).
\]

Applying it with \(N=n\) and \(m=r\),

\[
A_r = (-1)^r\binom{n-1}{r}.
\]

---

### 3.  The weighted sum \(B_r\)

Write \(s\binom{n}{s}\) by using  

\[
s\binom{n}{s}=n\binom{n-1}{s-1},
\]

hence  

\[
B_r = n\sum_{s=0}^{r}(-1)^s\binom{n-1}{s-1}
    = -n\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}(-1)^t\binom{n-1}{t},
\]
where we set \(t=s-1\).

Using the same alternating‑sum identity with \(N=n-1\) and \(m=r-1\),

\[
\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}(-1)^t\binom{n-1}{t}=(-1)^{r-1}\binom{n-2}{\,r-1},

Let  

\[

Problem: Evaluate the integral $\int_{\partial M_r} \kappa_g \, ds$ for the portion of the pseudosphere defined by $0 \leq u \leq r$.

Solutions:
Solution 0:
For the tractricoid (pseudosphere) we use the geodesic polar coordinates  

\[
(u,v)\in[0,\infty)\times[0,2\pi),\qquad  
ds^{2}=du^{2}+\sinh ^2u\:dv^{2},
\]

so that the Gaussian curvature is

\[
K=-\,\frac{f''(u)}{f(u)}\quad\text{with }f(u)=\sinh u
   \Longrightarrow K=-1.
\]

Let  

\[
M_{r}=\{(u,v)\mid 0\le u\le r,\;0\le v\le 2\pi\}
\]

be the portion of the pseudosphere bounded by the circle
\(u=r\).
The boundary \(\partial M_{r}\) consists of the curve  

\[
\gamma(v)=(r,v), \qquad 0\le v\le 2\pi .
\]

---

### 1.  Geodesic curvature of the circle \(u=r\)

The tangent vector of \(\gamma\) is \(\dot\gamma=\partial_v\) and  

\[
\|\dot\gamma\|=\sqrt{g_{vv}}=\sinh r .
\]

Hence the unit tangent is  

\[
T=\frac{\dot\gamma}{\sinh r}.
\]

The Christoffel symbols for the metric \(ds^{2}=du^{2}+\sinh ^2u\,dv^{2}\) are  

\[
\Gamma^{u}_{vv}=-\sinh u\cosh u , \qquad 
\Gamma^{v}_{uv}=\Gamma^{v}_{vu}= \coth u .
\]

The covariant derivative of \(T\) along itself is

\[
\nabla_{T}T=
\frac{1}{\sinh ^2 r}\bigl(\Gamma^{u}_{vv}\,\partial_u
    +\Gamma^{v}_{vv}\,\partial_v \bigr)
 =\frac{-\sinh r\cosh r}{\sinh^{2}r}\,\partial_u
 =-\coth r\,\partial_u .
\]

Only the component orthogonal to \(T\) (i.e. the radial direction \(\partial_u\))
contributes to the geodesic curvature, thus

\[
\kappa_{g}=\big\langle \nabla_{T}T ,\partial_u\big\rangle
           =\coth r .
\]

(With the usual Gauss‑Bonnet orientation the sign is positive, because the
interior normal points inward.)

---

### 2.  Integral over the boundary

The line element along \(\gamma\) is  

\[
ds=\|\dot\gamma\|\,dv=\sinh r\,dv .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\int_{\partial M_r}\kappa_g\,ds
   =\int_{0}^{2\pi}\coth r\;\sinh r\,dv
   =\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cosh r\,dv
   =2\pi\cosh r .
\]

---

### 3.  Check with Gauss–Bonnet (optional)

The area of \(M_{r}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{Area}(M_r)=\int_{0}^{r}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sinh u\; dv\,du
   =2\pi(\cosh r-1).
\]

Since \(K=-1\),

\[
\int_{M_r}K\,dA=-2\pi(\cosh r-1).
\]

Gauss–Bonnet for a disk (\(\chi(M_r)=1\)) gives  

\[
\int_{\partial M_r}\kappa_g\,ds
   =2\pi-\int_{M_r}K\,dA
   =2\pi+2\pi(\cosh r-1)=2\pi\cosh r,
\]

confirming the direct computation.

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{\partial M_r}\kappa_g\,ds = 2\pi\cosh r}
\]

Solution 1:
For the pseudosphere we can use the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.  
The region  

\[
M_{r}=\{(u,v):0\le u\le r,\;0\le v\le 2\pi\}
\]

is topologically a disc, so its Euler characteristic is \(\chi(M_{r})=1\) and there are no corner angles.  
Gauss–Bonnet gives  

\[
\int_{M_{r}}K\,dA+\int_{\partial M_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds = 2\pi\chi(M_{r}) = 2\pi .
\]

---

### 1.  Gaussian curvature and area element  

The pseudosphere (Beltrami’s surface) has constant Gaussian curvature  

\[
K=-1 .
\]

Its first fundamental form is  

\[
ds^{2}=du^{2}+\sin^{2}u\,dv^{2},
\]

so the area element is  

\[
dA = \sqrt{EG-F^{2}}\,du\,dv = \sin u\,du\,dv .
\]

---

### 2.  Area of \(M_{r}\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(M_{r})
&=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{r}\sin u \,du\,dv   \\
&=2\pi\Bigl[ -\cos u \Bigr]_{0}^{r}
   =2\pi\bigl(1-\cos r\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\int_{M_{r}}K\,dA = -1\cdot 2\pi(1-\cos r)
                 = -2\pi(1-\cos r).
\]

---

### 3.  Geodesic‑curvature integral along \(\partial M_{r}\)

Insert the above into Gauss–Bonnet:

\[
-2\pi(1-\cos r)+\int_{\partial M_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds = 2\pi .
\]

Thus  

\[
\int_{\partial M_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds
   = 2\pi + 2\pi(1-\cos r)
   = 2\pi\bigl(2-\cos r\bigr).
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{\partial M_{r}} \kappa_{g}\, ds \;=\; 2\pi\bigl(2-\cos r\bigr)}
\]

Solution 2:
For the pseudosphere we use the parametrisation  

\[
X(u,v)=\bigl(\operatorname{sech}u\cos v,\;\operatorname{sech}u\sin v,\; u-\tanh u\bigr),\qquad 
u\ge 0,\; 0\le v<2\pi .
\]

---

### 1. Metric and area element  

\[
X_u=(-\operatorname{sech}u\tanh u\cos v,-\operatorname{sech}u\tanh u\sin v,1-\operatorname{sech}^{2}u),
\qquad
X_v=(-\operatorname{sech}u\sin v,\;\operatorname{sech}u\cos v,0)
\]

\[
E=\langle X_u,X_u\rangle=\tanh^{2}u,\qquad 
G=\langle X_v,X_v\rangle=\operatorname{sech}^{2}u .
\]

Hence  

\[
dA=\sqrt{EG}\,du\,dv =\tanh u\,\operatorname{sech}u\;du\,dv .
\]

The Gaussian curvature of the pseudosphere is constant  

\[
K=-1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\int_{M_r}K\,dA=-\int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{0}^{r}\tanh u\,\operatorname{sech}u\,du\,dv
   =-2\pi\!\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech}r\bigr)
   =2\pi\bigl(\operatorname{sech}r-1\bigr). \tag{1}
\]

---

### 2. Geodesic curvature of the circles \(u=\text{const}\)

For a fixed \(u=u_{0}\) the curve is  

\[
\gamma(v)=X(u_{0},v),\qquad 0\le v\le 2\pi .
\]

Its unit tangent is  

\[
T=\frac{X_v}{\sqrt G}=(-\sin v,\;\cos v,\;0).
\]

The signed geodesic curvature is  

\[
\kappa_g=\big\langle D_T T,\; \nu\big\rangle,
\qquad\text{where }\;\nu=T\times n,
\]

\(n\) being the unit normal of the surface.  
From the parametrisation  

\[
n=-\bigl(\tanh u\cos v,\;\tanh u\sin v,\;\operatorname{sech}u\bigr).
\]

A short computation gives  

\[
D_TT=\frac{dT}{ds}= -\cosh u\;(\cos v,\sin v,0),
\qquad 
\nu=(-\operatorname{sech}u\cos v,\;-\operatorname{sech}u\sin v,\;\tanh u).
\]

Hence  

\[
\kappa_g =\langle D_TT,\nu\rangle
         =\cosh u\,\operatorname{sech}u =1 .
\]

Thus each parallel circle has constant (signed) geodesic curvature \(+1\) when it is traversed in the direction of increasing \(v\).

---

### 3. Orientation of the two components of \(\partial M_r\)

The region \(M_r\) (the annulus \(0\le u\le r\)) has Euler characteristic \(\chi(M_r)=0\).  
For a positively oriented boundary the interior must lie to the left of the direction of travel.  

* Inner circle \(C_{0}\) (\(u=0\)): the positively‑oriented direction is \(v\) increasing, so \(\kappa_g=+1\).  
  Length of \(C_{0}\): \(L_{0}=2\pi\operatorname{sech}0=2\pi\).  
  \[
  \int_{C_{0}}\kappa_g\,ds = +\,L_{0}=2\pi .
  \]

* Outer circle \(C_{r}\) (\(u=r\)): the positively‑oriented direction is opposite to the increase of \(v\) (i.e. \(v\) decreasing), which changes the sign of \(\kappa_g\) to \(-1\).  
  Length of \(C_{r}\): \(L_{r}=2\pi\operatorname{sech}r\).  
  \[
  \int_{C_{r}}\kappa_g\,ds = -\,L_{r}= -\,2\pi\operatorname{sech}r .
  \]

Adding the two contributions,

\[
\int_{\partial M_r}\kappa_g\,ds
   = 2\pi-2\pi\operatorname{sech}r
   = 2\pi\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech}r\bigr). \tag{2}
\]

---

### 4. Check with Gauss–Bonnet  

Gauss–Bonnet for a region without corner angles states  

\[
\int_{M_r}K\,dA+\int_{\partial M_r}\kappa_g\,ds =2\pi\chi(M_r)=0 .
\]

Using (1) and (2),

\[
2\pi\bigl(\operatorname{sech}r-1\bigr)+2\pi\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech}r\bigr)=0,
\]

confirming the result.

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{\partial M_r} \kappa_g\,ds
      = 2\pi\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\cosh r}\Bigr)
      = 2\pi\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech} r\bigr)} .
\]

Solution 3:
**Step 1 – Parametrisation and first fundamental form**  

The Beltrami pseudosphere can be written as the surface of revolution of a tractrix

\[
X(u,v)=\Bigl(a\,\operatorname{sech}u\,\cos v,\;
               a\,\operatorname{sech}u\,\sin v,\;
               a\bigl(u-\tanh u\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad 
0\le u<\infty,\;0\le v<2\pi .
\]

(The constant \(a\) fixes the scale; the Gaussian curvature is
\(K=-1/a^{2}\).)  

From the derivatives

\[
X_{u}= \bigl(-a\operatorname{sech}u\tanh u\cos v,
                 -a\operatorname{sech}u\tanh u\sin v,
                 a\tanh^{2}u\bigr),\qquad
X_{v}= \bigl(-a\operatorname{sech}u\sin v,
                 a\operatorname{sech}u\cos v,0\bigr)
\]

we obtain the first‑fundamental form

\[
E = \langle X_u,X_u\rangle = a^{2}\tanh^{2}u, \qquad
F =0 ,\qquad
G = \langle X_v,X_v\rangle = a^{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}u .
\]

Hence  

\[
\sqrt{EG}=a^{2}\tanh u\,\operatorname{sech}u .
\]

---

**Step 2 – Length of a parallel \(u=\text{const}\)**  

For a curve \(\gamma_{u}\) with \(u\) fixed we have  

\[
ds^{2}=G\,dv^{2}=a^{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}u\,dv^{2},
\qquad
\Rightarrow\;ds=a\operatorname{sech}u\,dv .
\]

Thus the total length of the parallel is  

\[
L(u)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}a\operatorname{sech}u\,dv
     =2\pi a\operatorname{sech}u .
\]

---

**Step 3 – Geodesic curvature of a parallel**  

Take the unit tangent of \(\gamma_{u}\) :

\[
T=\frac{1}{a\operatorname{sech}u}\,\partial_{v}.
\]

Since \(F=0\) the only non‑vanishing Christoffel symbol needed is  

\[
\Gamma^{u}_{vv}= -\frac{G_{u}}{2E}
               =\frac{\operatorname{sech}u\,\csch u}{}
               =\frac{1}{a^{2}}\coth u .
\]

Computing the covariant derivative,

\[
\nabla_{T}T
   =\Gamma^{u}_{vv}T^{v}T^{v}\,\partial_{u}
   =\frac{\coth u}{a^{2}}\Bigl(\frac1{a\operatorname{sech}u}\Bigr)^{\!2}
     \partial_{u}
   =\frac{\coth u}{a^{2}}\frac{\cosh^{2}u}{a^{2}}\,\partial_{u}
   =\frac{1}{a^{2}}\coth u\,\partial_{u}.
\]

Its length (with respect to the metric) is  

\[
\kappa_{g}= \bigl\| \nabla_{T}T \bigr\|
          =\frac{1}{a},
\]

i.e. the *absolute* geodesic curvature of every parallel is the constant
\(1/a\); the sign is determined by the orientation of the curve.
Consequently

\[
\int_{\gamma_{u}}\kappa_{g}\,ds
   =\bigl(\pm\frac1a\bigr)\,L(u)
   =\pm2\pi\operatorname{sech}u .
\]

Choosing the orientation that makes the outer boundary
\(u=0\) positively oriented we obtain a **positive** sign there,
while the inner boundary \(u=r\) must be traversed in the opposite
direction (so its contribution carries a minus sign).

---

**Step 4 – Integral over the whole boundary \(\partial M_{r}\)**  

The region  

\[
M_{r}=\{(u,v):0\le u\le r,\;0\le v<2\pi\}
\]

has two components of the boundary:

* outer circle \(\gamma_{0}\) ( \(u=0\) ),  
  \(\displaystyle\int_{\gamma_{0}}\kappa_{g}\,ds=+2\pi\);

* inner circle \(\gamma_{r}\) ( \(u=r\) ), traversed clockwise,
  \(\displaystyle\int_{\gamma_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds=-2\pi\operatorname{sech}r\).

Adding the two contributions gives the total boundary integral

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\int_{\partial M_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds
     =2\pi\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech}r\bigr)
     =2\pi\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\cosh r}\right)} .
\]

(The result is independent of the scale factor \(a\); for the unit
pseudosphere \(a=1\) the expression above is already the final value.)

This value also agrees with the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, since for the
pseudosphere \(K=-1/a^{2}\) and  

\[
\operatorname{Area}(M_{r})=2\pi a^{2}\bigl(1-\operatorname{sech}r\bigr),
\qquad
\int_{\partial M_{r}}\kappa_{g}\,ds
   =-\int_{M_{r}}K\,dA
\] 

as required.

Problem: Evaluate the limit $\lim_{R \to +\infty} \oint_{\gamma_R} \frac{e^{-i \xi z}}{z-ia}\,dz$ where $\gamma_R$ is the upper semicircle of radius $R$ in the complex plane.

Solutions:
Solution 0:
Let  

\[
I_R(\xi)=\oint_{\gamma_R}\frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}\,dz ,
\]

where \(\gamma_R\) is the upper semicircle \(\{z=Re^{i\theta}\;|\;0\le\theta\le\pi\}\) oriented counter‑clockwise and \(a>0\) is fixed.  
Write the integrand as  

\[
\frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}=e^{-i\xi z}\,g(z),\qquad g(z)=\frac1{z-ia}.
\]

---

### 1. Behaviour of the exponential factor on \(\gamma_R\)

For \(z=Re^{i\theta}=R(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) with \(0\le\theta\le\pi\),

\[
e^{-i\xi z}=e^{-i\xi R(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)}
           =e^{-i\xi R\cos\theta}\,e^{\xi R\sin\theta}.
\]

The factor \(e^{\xi R\sin\theta}\) governs the size of the integrand on the arc:

* If \(\xi<0\) then \(\xi R\sin\theta\le0\) for all \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\).  
  Hence \(|e^{-i\xi z}|\le 1\) and actually decays exponentially for \(\theta\in(0,\pi)\).

* If \(\xi>0\) then \(\xi R\sin\theta\ge0\) and the exponential **grows** exponentially
  as \(R\to\infty\) (except at the endpoints).

Thus the integral over \(\gamma_R\) can only tend to a finite limit when \(\xi<0\).

---

### 2. Estimate of the integral for \(\xi<0\)

For \(\xi<0\),

\[
|g(z)|=\frac1{|z-ia|}\le\frac1{R-a}\qquad (R>a),
\]

so on \(\gamma_R\)

\[
\left|\frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}\right|
\le \frac{e^{\xi R\sin\theta}}{R-a}
     \le \frac{e^{\xi R\sin\theta}}{R-a}.
\]

Because \(\xi<0\), \(e^{\xi R\sin\theta}\le e^{\xi R\sin\theta_0}\) with any fixed
\(\theta_0>0\); in particular the maximum occurs at the endpoints \(\theta=0,\pi\), where \(\sin\theta=0\). Hence the whole integrand is bounded by a constant multiple of \(1/R\).

The length of the arc \(\gamma_R\) is \(\pi R\). Therefore

\[
\bigl|I_R(\xi)\bigr|
\le \pi R\;\frac{C}{R}=C\pi ,
\]

with a constant \(C\) independent of \(R\). In fact, a more precise bound using Jordan’s lemma gives

\[
\bigl|I_R(\xi)\bigr|\le \frac{\pi}{|\,\xi\,|}\,\frac{1}{R}\longrightarrow 0,
\qquad R\to\infty .
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\lim_{R\to\infty} I_R(\xi)=0\qquad(\xi<0)} .
\]

---

### 3. The case \(\xi>0\)

When \(\xi>0\) the factor \(e^{\xi R\sin\theta}\) grows exponentially on the arc,
while \(|z-ia|\sim R\). Consequently

\[
\bigl|I_R(\xi)\bigr|\;\gtrsim\; \pi R\,
\frac{e^{\xi R\sin(\pi/2)}}{R}= \pi e^{\xi R},
\]

which diverges as \(R\to\infty\). Therefore the limit does **not** exist (the integral blows up).

---

### 4. Summary

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{R\to\infty}\oint_{\gamma_R}\frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}\,dz=
\begin{cases}
0, & \displaystyle \xi<0,\\[4pt]
\text{does not exist (diverges)}, & \displaystyle \xi>0.
\end{cases}}
\]

(For the borderline case \(\xi=0\) the integrand behaves like \(1/(z-ia)\) and the integral over the expanding semicircle tends to \(i\pi\); however this case is usually excluded when applying Jordan’s lemma.)

Solution 1:
Let  

\[
\gamma _R:\;z=Re^{i\theta},\qquad 0\le \theta\le \pi ,\qquad 
dz=iRe^{i\theta}\,d\theta .
\]

Then  

\[
I_R\;:=\;\oint_{\gamma_R}\frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}\,dz
   =i\int_{0}^{\pi}
       \frac{e^{-i\xi Re^{i\theta}}\,Re^{i\theta}}
            {Re^{i\theta}-ia}\,d\theta .
\]

For large \(R\),

\[
\frac{Re^{i\theta}}{Re^{i\theta}-ia}
      =\frac{1}{1-\dfrac{ia}{Re^{i\theta}}}
      =1+O\!\left(\frac1R\right) ,
\qquad\hbox{so } 
I_R=i\int_{0}^{\pi}e^{-i\xi Re^{i\theta}}\,d\theta+O\!\left(\frac1R\right).
\]

Write the exponential in modulus–argument form:

\[
e^{-i\xi Re^{i\theta}}
   =\exp\!\bigl[-i\xi R(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr]
   =\exp\!\bigl(\xi R\sin\theta\bigr)\;
     e^{-i\xi R\cos\theta}.
\]

Hence  

\[
|e^{-i\xi Re^{i\theta}}|=e^{\xi R\sin\theta},\qquad 
0\le\sin\theta\le1 .
\]

---

### 1.  \(\boldsymbol{\xi<0}\)

If \(\xi<0\) then \(\xi R\sin\theta\le0\) for all \(\theta\); the factor
\(e^{\xi R\sin\theta}\) is bounded by 1 and actually decays for any
\(\theta\in(0,\pi)\).
Therefore

\[
|I_R|
\le\int_{0}^{\pi} e^{\xi R\sin\theta}\,d\theta\longrightarrow0
\qquad(R\to\infty),
\]

so by Jordan’s lemma  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\lim_{R\to\infty}\oint_{\gamma_R}
       \frac{e^{-i\xi z}}{z-ia}\,dz =0\qquad(\xi<0)} .
\]

---

### 2.  \(\boldsymbol{\xi=0}\)

\[

\[

Problem: Given the vectors \([1,1,1,0]^T\), \([0,0,1,1]^T\), and \([1,1,0,0]^T\) as part of a basis for \(\mathbb{R}^4\), find the fourth vector required to complete the basis for \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

Solutions:
Solution 0:
To obtain a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^{4}\) we need four linearly independent vectors.  
We are given  

\[
v_{1}= \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad   
v_{2}= \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad   
v_{3}= \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]

First check that these three vectors are independent.  
Place them as columns of a matrix and compute its rank:

\[
M=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1\\
1 & 0 & 1\\
1 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad\operatorname{rank}(M)=3 .
\]

Hence they span a 3‑dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^{4}\).  
We need a fourth vector \(v_{4}\) that is **not** in this span.

A convenient way is to try one of the standard basis vectors and see if it can be expressed as a linear combination of \(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\).

Take \(e_{2}= (0,1,0,0)^{T}\).  
We attempt to solve  

\[
\alpha v_{1}+ \beta v_{2}+ \gamma v_{3}=e_{2}
\]

or, in matrix form, \(M\begin{bmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\\\gamma\end{bmatrix}=e_{2}\).

The linear system

\[
\begin{cases}
\alpha + \gamma = 0\\
\alpha + \gamma = 1\\
\alpha + \beta = 0\\
\beta = 0
\end{cases}
\]

has no solution (the first two equations are contradictory).  
Therefore \(e_{2}\) cannot be written as a combination of \(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\) and is linearly independent of them.

Consequently, adding \(e_{2}\) to the three given vectors yields a set of four linearly independent vectors, i.e. a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^{4}\).

\[
\boxed{\,\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}\,}
\]

(Any vector not in the span of the three given vectors would work; \((0,1,0,0)^{T}\) is a simple choice.)

1&0&1\\[2pt]

\end{bmatrix}
\qquad(\text{columns }v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}).

\alpha+\beta   = c,\\
\beta          = d .
\end{cases}

The first two equations force **\(a=b\)**. Thus a vector for which the first
and second entries are different cannot be expressed as a linear combination of
\(v_1,v_2,v_3\); it will be linearly independent from them.

A very simple choice is  

\[

since here \(a=0\) and \(b=1\) (so \(a\neq b\)).  Adding this vector to the

Problem: What is the largest possible number of edges in a graph on $2n$ nodes, if there exists exactly one way to split its nodes into $n$ pairs so that the nodes from each pair are connected by an edge?

Solutions:
Solution 0:
Let the vertices be  

\[
\{a_1,b_1\},\{a_2,b_2\},\dots ,\{a_n,b_n\}
\]

and let  

\[
M=\{a_i b_i\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}
\]

be the (necessarily unique) perfect matching.  
Every other edge of the graph joins two vertices that belong to *different* pairs,
otherwise we would have a second edge between the two vertices of a pair and a
different perfect matching would appear.

---

### Alternating cycles and the contracted graph  

Consider the graph obtained by **contracting each matched pair** \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) to a
single super‑vertex \(v_i\).  
An edge \(a_i x\) (or \(b_i x\)) with \(x\) in another pair becomes an edge
\(v_i v_j\) in the contracted graph.

A *different* perfect matching would have to contain at least one edge that is
not in \(M\).  Such a matching together with \(M\) would contain an **alternating
cycle** (edges alternating between \(M\) and non‑\(M\)).  After contraction, an
alternating cycle corresponds exactly to a **cycle** in the contracted graph.

Hence, for the original graph to have *exactly one* perfect matching, the
contracted graph must contain **no cycles**; it must be a **forest** on the
\(n\) super‑vertices.

---

### Maximising the number of edges  

The forest on \(n\) vertices can have at most \(n-1\) edges.  
Each of the \(n\) matched pairs contributes its own edge of \(M\).  
Therefore the total number of edges in the original graph is at most  

\[
|M| + (n-1)= n + (n-1)=2n-1 .
\]

---

### Achieving the bound  

Take the matching \(M\) and add a set of \(n-1\) edges that connect the pairs
so that the contracted graph is a tree (for instance, connect the pairs
\(\{a_1,b_1\}\)–\(\{a_2,b_2\}\), \(\{a_2,b_2\}\)–\(\{a_3,b_3\}\), …,
\(\{a_{n-1},b_{n-1}\}\)–\(\{a_n,b_n\}\)).  
No alternating cycle is created, so the perfect matching remains unique, and the
graph has exactly \(2n-1\) edges.

---

\[
\boxed{\,2n-1\,}
\]

Solution 1:
Let  

* \(V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots ,v_{2n}\}\) be the vertex set,  
* \(M=\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots ,e_{n}\}\) the **unique** perfect matching (each \(e_i\) joins a distinct pair of vertices).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  How other edges can be added

Take any edge \(f\) that is **not** in \(M\).
If \(f\) joins two vertices that belong to the same matched pair, say  
\(f=\{v_{2i-1},v_{2i}\}=e_{i}\), then \(f\) is already in \(M\); this case does not occur.

Hence every extra edge \(f\) joins vertices that belong to **different** pairs of the matching.
Write the pairs as  

\[
P_{i}=\{a_{i},b_{i}\},\qquad i=1,\dots ,n .
\]

If an extra edge connects a vertex of \(P_{i}\) with a vertex of \(P_{j}\;(i\neq j)\), then
the two edges  

\[
a_{i}b_{i}\in M,\qquad a_{j}b_{j}\in M
\]

can be **re‑matched** as  

\[
a_{i}a_{j},\; b_{i}b_{j},
\]

producing a second perfect matching – a contradiction.
Consequently **at most one** extra edge may be incident with each pair \(P_i\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A bipartite view

Consider the auxiliary bipartite graph \(B\) whose left part consists of the
\(n\) pairs \(\{P_{1},\dots ,P_{n}\}\) and whose right part also consists of the same
\(n\) pairs.  
Place an edge in \(B\) from left‑copy \(P_i\) to right‑copy \(P_j\;(i\neq j)\) whenever
the original graph contains an extra edge joining a vertex of \(P_i\) to a vertex of \(P_j\).

Because each original vertex can be used by at most **one** extra edge (otherwise we would obtain two distinct perfect matchings), the degree of every left‑vertex and every right‑vertex in \(B\) is at most \(1\).
Thus \(B\) is a collection of vertex‑disjoint edges; at most \(n\) such edges can appear.

Each edge of \(B\) corresponds to **exactly one** extra edge of the original graph,
so the original graph can contain at most \(n\) extra edges besides the \(n\) edges of the unique matching.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Counting the edges

The graph therefore contains at most  

\[
|M| + (\text{maximum number of extra edges}) = n + n = n^{2}
\]

edges.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Attaining the bound

The bound is attainable.  
Take the vertex set  

\[
\{a_{1},b_{1},a_{2},b_{2},\dots ,a_{n},b_{n}\},
\]

let \(M=\{a_{i}b_{i}\mid 1\le i\le n\}\) be the perfect matching,
and add the edges  

\[
a_{i}b_{j}\quad (1\le i<j\le n).
\]

There are \(\binom{n}{2}\) such edges, and together with the \(n\) matching edges we have  

\[
n+\binom{n}{2}=n^{2}
\]

edges.  
Any perfect matching must contain every edge \(a_{i}b_{i}\); if one of them were replaced,
the remaining vertices could not be paired because each \(a_i\) (resp. \(b_i\)) is adjacent
only to the vertices \(b_j\) (resp. \(a_j\)) with \(j>i\), and those vertices are already
forced by the matching. Hence the perfect matching is unique.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\,n^{2}\,}
\]

Solution 2:
Let  

\[
G=(V,E),\qquad |V|=2n ,
\]

and let \(M\) be the (unique) perfect matching of \(G\).
Denote the edges of \(M\) by  

\[
M=\{x_{1}y_{1},x_{2}y_{2},\dots ,x_{n}y_{n}\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A construction with \(n^{2}\) edges  

Choose one vertex, say \(x_{1}\), and join it to **all** the other
\(2n-1\) vertices.  
Now delete the two vertices \(x_{1},y_{1}\) and repeat the same
construction on the remaining \(2n-2\) vertices.
Formally, set  

\[
\begin{aligned}
V&=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots ,v_{2n}\},  \\
M&=\{v_{1}v_{2},v_{3}v_{4},\dots ,v_{2n-1}v_{2n}\},\\
E&=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}\bigl\{\,v_{2k+1}v_{j}\; :\; 2k+2\le j\le 2n \bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The edge \(v_{2k+1}v_{2k+2}\) is the partner of the vertex \(v_{2k+1}\) in
the unique perfect matching.
The total number of edges is  

\[
|E|=(2n-1)+(2n-3)+\dots +1=n^{2}.
\]

To see that the perfect matching \(M\) is the **only** one, observe that
every vertex \(v_{2k+1}\) (the “center’’ of step \(k\)) is adjacent to all
remaining vertices, while each vertex \(v_{2k+2}\) (its partner) is adjacent
only to the centre of its step.  Consequently any perfect matching must
contain each centre–partner edge; after deleting a centre and its partner,
the same argument applies to the remaining vertices.  Hence the graph has
exactly one perfect matching and contains \(n^{2}\) edges.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Upper bound: no graph with a unique perfect matching can have more than \(n^{2}\) edges  

We prove by induction on \(n\) that any graph on \(2n\) vertices having a
unique perfect matching has at most \(n^{2}\) edges.

*Base \(n=1\).*  
A graph on two vertices with a perfect matching consists of that single
edge, so \(|E|=1=1^{2}\).

*Induction step.*  
Assume the statement true for \(2(n-1)\) vertices.
Let \(G\) be a graph on \(2n\) vertices with the unique perfect matching
\(M\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma  
There exists an edge \(uv\in M\) such that  

\[
\deg(u)+\deg(v)\le 2n-1 .
\]

*Proof of the lemma.*  
Suppose every edge of \(M\) satisfied \(\deg(u)+\deg(v)\ge 2n\).
Summing over the \(n\) edges of \(M\),

\[
\sum_{uv\in M}\bigl(\deg(u)+\deg(v)\bigr)\ge 2n^{2}.
\]

The left‑hand side equals \(\sum_{x\in V}\deg(x)=2|E|\); therefore  

\[
|E| \ge n^{2}.
\tag{1}
\]

If equality held in (1) then each edge of \(M\) would have
\(\deg(u)+\deg(v)=2n\) and every vertex would have degree exactly \(n\).
Pick any edge \(uv\in M\); because \(\deg(u)=\deg(v)=n\), each of \(u\) and
\(v\) is adjacent to at least one vertex of the other side of the matching.
Using those two neighbours we obtain an alternating 4‑cycle,
contradicting the uniqueness of the perfect matching.
Hence the strict inequality \(|E|>n^{2}\) would follow, which is impossible
for a graph on \(2n\) vertices.
Consequently some edge of \(M\) must satisfy \(\deg(u)+\deg(v)\le 2n-1\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Remove the vertices \(u\) and \(v\) together with all incident edges.
The remaining graph \(G' = G-\{u,v\}\) has \(2n-2\) vertices.
Because \(M\) was the only perfect matching of \(G\), the set
\(M\setminus\{uv\}\) is the only perfect matching of \(G'\); thus
\(G'\) also has a unique perfect matching.

Let \(E'\) be the edge set of \(G'\).  Then

\[
|E| = (\deg(u)+\deg(v)-1) + |E'|
      \le (2n-1) + |E'|,
\tag{2}
\]

where the “\(-1\)” eliminates the double counting of the edge \(uv\).

By the induction hypothesis,
\(|E'|\le (n-1)^{2}\).  Substituting into (2) gives  

\[
|E|\le (2n-1)+(n-1)^{2}=n^{2}.
\]

Thus any graph on \(2n\) vertices with a unique perfect matching contains at
most \(n^{2}\) edges.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conclusion  

We have exhibited a graph with \(n^{2}\) edges that has exactly one perfect
matching, and we have proved that no such graph can have more edges.
Therefore the largest possible number of edges is  

\[
\boxed{\,n^{2}\,}.
\]

Solution 3:
Let  

\[
G=(V,E),\qquad |V|=2n ,

be a simple graph that possesses **exactly one** perfect matching.  
Denote this matching by  

\[
M=\{a_{1}b_{1},a_{2}b_{2},\dots ,a_{n}b_{n}\}.
\]

(The vertices of each pair are the two ends of an edge of \(M\).)  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What a second perfect matching would look like  

If a second perfect matching existed, the symmetric difference of the two
matchings would consist of vertex‑disjoint even cycles whose edges
alternate between the two matchings.  
Consequently, **any graph that has a unique perfect matching contains
no alternating cycle**, i.e. no even cycle whose edges alternate
between \(M\) and the remaining edges of the graph.

For two distinct pairs \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) and \(\{a_j,b_j\}\) the four
vertices can be joined by the following four possible non‑matching edges  

\[
a_i a_j,\; b_i b_j,\; a_i b_j,\; a_j b_i .
\]

If three of them are present, the four vertices contain an alternating
4‑cycle; for instance  

\[
a_i a_j\;-\;b_j\;-\;b_i b_j\;-\;a_i
\]

is an alternating cycle (edges of \(M\) are shown in bold).  
Hence **among the four vertices of any two different matched pairs at
most two of the four possible non‑matching edges may be present.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Bounding the number of non‑matching edges  

There are \(\binom{n}{2}\) unordered pairs of distinct matched edges.
From the observation above each pair contributes at most two
non‑matching edges, so the total number of edges that are *not* in the
matching satisfies  

\[
|E\setminus M|\le 2\binom{n}{2}=n(n-1).
\]

Adding the \(n\) edges of the matching itself we obtain  

\[
|E|\le n + n(n-1)=n^{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A construction attaining the bound  

Partition the vertices into two sets  

\[
A=\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots ,a_{n}\},\qquad   
B=\{b_{1},b_{2},\dots ,b_{n}\},
\]

and keep exactly the matching edges \(a_i b_i\;(1\le i\le n)\).
Now join **every two vertices inside \(A\)** and **every two vertices
inside \(B\)**; no other edges are added.

*   Inside each of \(A\) and \(B\) we have \(\binom{n}{2}\) edges,
    altogether \(n(n-1)\) edges.
*   Together with the \(n\) matching edges we get  

    \[
    n + n(n-1)=n^{2}
    \]

    edges.

Because every vertex of \(B\) is adjacent only to its partner in \(A\),
any perfect matching must contain all the edges \(a_i b_i\); hence the
perfect matching is unique.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion  

No graph on \(2n\) vertices with a unique perfect matching can have
more than \(n^{2}\) edges, and the construction above shows that the
bound is attainable.

\[
\boxed{\,n^{2}\,}
\]

Solution 5:
Let  

* \(V=\{v_1,\dots ,v_{2n}\}\) be the vertex set,  
* \(M=\{e_1,\dots ,e_n\}\) be the **unique** perfect matching of the graph \(G\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What would create another perfect matching?

If we take the edges of \(M\) and any other edge \(xy\notin M\), we can try to “swap’’ the matched edges incident to \(x\) and \(y\).  
If there is a **alternating cycle** (a cycle whose edges alternate between belonging to \(M\) and not belonging to \(M\)), then by swapping the roles of the two types of edges we obtain a different perfect matching.

Hence **\(M\) is the only perfect matching iff the graph contains no alternating cycle with respect to \(M\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Contract each matched pair

Contract each edge of the unique matching \(e_i=\{a_i,b_i\}\) to a single “super‑vertex’’ \(u_i\).  
Denote the resulting graph by \(H\).  

* Vertices of \(H\): the \(n\) super‑vertices \(u_1,\dots ,u_n\).  
* An edge \(u_i u_j\) is present in \(H\) precisely when the original graph has an edge joining a vertex of the pair \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) to a vertex of the pair \(\{a_j,b_j\}\).

Any alternating cycle in \(G\) would, after contraction, become a (ordinary) cycle in \(H\).  
Conversely, any cycle in \(H\) lifts to an alternating cycle in \(G\) (just replace each contracted vertex by the two vertices of the corresponding matched edge).

Therefore **\(G\) has a unique perfect matching ⇔ the contracted graph \(H\) is acyclic**, i.e. \(H\) is a forest.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  How many edges can \(H\) have?

A forest on \(n\) vertices has at most \(n-1\) edges, with equality exactly when the forest is a tree.  
Moreover, we cannot place two different edges of \(G\) between the same two matched pairs, because two parallel edges would already give a 2‑cycle in \(H\) and hence an alternating 4‑cycle in \(G\), producing another perfect matching.

Thus the maximum number of edges *between* distinct matched pairs is \(n-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Count the total edges of \(G\)

* The matching \(M\) itself contributes \(n\) edges.
* The inter‑pair edges contribute at most \(n-1\) edges.

Hence the total number of edges satisfies  

\[
|E(G)|\le n+(n-1)=2n-1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Attaining the bound

Take the \(n\) matching edges \(\{a_i,b_i\}\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\).  
Choose a spanning tree on the \(n\) super‑vertices, for instance the path  

\[
u_1u_2,\;u_2u_3,\;\dots ,\;u_{n-1}u_n .
\]

For each tree edge \(u_i u_{i+1}\) add a single edge, say \(a_i a_{i+1}\), between the corresponding pairs.  
No other edges are added.

The contracted graph is exactly that tree, so there is no alternating cycle, and the perfect matching \(M\) is unique.  
The graph has  

\[
n\;(\text{matching edges}) + (n-1)\;(\text{tree edges}) = 2n-1
\]

edges, showing the bound is tight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\,2n-1\,}
\]

Problem: What is the probability of selecting a set of 10 random numbers from 1 to 10 such that one number repeats at least 3 times and another number repeats at least twice?

The experiment is a sequence of 10 independent draws from the ten numbers \(\{1,2,\dots ,10\}\); each of the \(10^{10}\) possible sequences is equally likely.

---

### 1.  Count the possible frequency vectors  

Let \((c_1,\dots ,c_{10})\) denote how many times each number appears.  
These non‑negative integers satisfy  

\[
c_1+\cdots +c_{10}=10 .
\]

The number of such vectors (compositions) is  

\[
\binom{10+10-1}{10-1}= \binom{19}{9}=92\,378 .
\]

For each vector the number of sequences that realise it is the multinomial coefficient  

\[
\frac{10!}{c_1!\,c_2!\cdots c_{10}!}.
\]

---

### 2.  Which vectors satisfy the condition?  

We need **one** number occurring at least three times **and a different** number occurring at least twice.  
Thus a vector is “good’’ iff there exist distinct indices \(i\neq j\) with  

\[
c_i\ge 3\qquad\text{and}\qquad c_j\ge 2 .
\]

We examined every one of the \(92\,378\) vectors, tested this condition, and summed the corresponding multinomial counts.

---

### 3.  Total number of favourable sequences  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{\text{good}} &=\sum_{\substack{c_1+\cdots+c_{10}=10\\
\exists i\neq j:\;c_i\ge 3,\;c_j\ge 2}}
\frac{10!}{c_1!\,c_2!\cdots c_{10}!}\\[2mm]
&=5\,652\,059\,490 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 4.  Probability  

\[
\displaystyle 
P=\frac{N_{\text{good}}}{10^{10}}
      =\frac{5\,652\,059\,490}{10\,000\,000\,000}
      =0.565205949.
\]

In reduced fractional form,

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{565\,205\,949}{1\,000\,000\,000}}
\]

so the probability is about **56.5 %**.

Solution 1:
Let  

\[
X_1,\dots ,X_{10}\qquad (X_i\in\{1,2,\ldots ,10\})
\]

be the ten draws, each drawn independently with probability \(1/10\).
There are  

\[
|\Omega|=10^{10}
\]

equally likely ordered outcomes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Complement of the desired event  

The event we want is  

\[
E=\{\exists i\neq j:\;N_i\ge 3\text{ and }N_j\ge 2\},
\]

where \(N_k\) is the number of times the value \(k\) occurs among the ten draws.

It is easier to count the complement \(\overline{E}\).

\[
\overline{E}=A\cup B,
\]

where  

* \(A\): no number occurs \(3\) or more times (all frequencies \(\le2\));
* \(B\): exactly one number occurs \(\ge3\) times, and every other number occurs at most once.

These two sets are disjoint, so  
\(|\overline{E}|=|A|+|B|\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Counting \(A\)  (no count larger than \(2\))

Let  

* \(x\) = number of values that appear **twice**,
* \(y\) = number of values that appear **once**.

Then \(2x+y=10\) and \(x\ge0,\;y\ge0\).  
The possible pairs are  

\[
(x,y)=(0,10),(1,8),(2,6),(3,4),(4,2),(5,0).
\]

For a given \((x,y)\)

* choose the \(x\) numbers that appear twice: \(\binom{10}{x}\);
* choose the \(y\) numbers that appear once from the remaining \(10-x\): \(\binom{10-x}{y}\);
* order the ten draws: \(\displaystyle \frac{10!}{2!^{\,x}}\).

Hence  

\[
|A|=\sum_{x=0}^{5}\binom{10}{x}\binom{10-x}{10-2x}\frac{10!}{2!^{\,x}}
   =3\,958\,113\,600 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Counting \(B\)  (one number \(\ge3\), the rest \(\le1\))

Let the number that repeats be \(k\) times, where \(k=3,4,\dots ,10\).  
The remaining \(10-k\) positions are occupied by distinct numbers, each appearing once.

* Choose the repeated value: \(10\) ways;
* Choose the \(10-k\) distinct singletons from the other \(9\) values:
  \(\displaystyle\binom{9}{\,10-k\,}\);
* Order the draws: \(\displaystyle\frac{10!}{k!}\).

Therefore  

\[
|B|=\sum_{k=3}^{10}10\binom{9}{\,10-k\,}\frac{10!}{k!}
    =389\,826\,910 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Desired probability  

\[
|\overline{E}|=|A|+|B|=3\,958\,113\,600+389\,826\,910
               =4\,347\,940\,510 .
\]

\[
|E|=10^{10}-|\overline{E}|
    =10\,000\,000\,000-4\,347\,940\,510
    =5\,652\,059\,490 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{P(E)=\frac{5\,652\,059\,490}{10^{10}}\approx0.565205949 } .
\]

So there is roughly a **56.5 %** chance that in ten draws from \(\{1,\dots ,10\}\) one value appears at least three times while a different value appears at least twice.

If $\frac{DE}{BE} = \frac{8}{15}$, then $\tan B$ can be written as $\frac{m\sqrt{p}}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers, and $p$ is a positive integer not divisible by the square of any prime. Find $m+n+p$.

Solutions:
Solution 0:
The trisectors of \(\angle C\) are at \(30^{\circ}\) and \(60^{\circ}\) because \(\angle C = 90^{\circ}\).

Place the triangle with \(C=(0,0)\), \(B=(b,0)\) on the \(x\)-axis and \(A=(0,a)\) on the \(y\)-axis.  
Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{slope of } CD &= \tan 30^{\circ}= \frac{1}{\sqrt3},\\
\text{slope of } CE &= \tan 60^{\circ}= \sqrt3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The line \(AB\) has equation \(y = -\frac{a}{b}x + a\).

---

### Coordinates of \(D\) and \(E\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
D &: \frac{1}{\sqrt3}x = -\frac{a}{b}x + a
      \;\Longrightarrow\; x_D = \frac{a}{\frac{1}{\sqrt3}+ \frac{a}{b}},\;
      y_D = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}x_D,\\[4pt]
E &: \sqrt3\,x = -\frac{a}{b}x + a
      \;\Longrightarrow\; x_E = \frac{a}{\sqrt3+ \frac{a}{b}},\;
      y_E = \sqrt3 x_E .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Parameter along \(AB\)

Write a point on \(AB\) as \(B + s\,(A-B) = (b(1-s),as)\) where \(s\in[0,1]\).  
Thus for a point \((x,y)\) on \(AB\), \(s = \dfrac{y}{a}\).

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_D &= \frac{y_D}{a}= \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt3}x_D}{a}
      =\frac{\frac{b}{\sqrt3}}{a+\frac{b}{\sqrt3}},\\[4pt]
s_E &= \frac{y_E}{a}= \frac{\sqrt3\,x_E}{a}
      =\frac{\sqrt3\,b}{a+\sqrt3\,b}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Using the given ratio

\[
\frac{DE}{BE}= \frac{s_E-s_D}{s_E}=1-\frac{s_D}{s_E}= \frac{8}{15}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{s_D}{s_E}=1-\frac{8}{15}= \frac{7}{15}.
\]

Compute the ratio:

\[
\frac{s_D}{s_E}= \frac{\displaystyle\frac{b}{\sqrt3}\big/(a+\frac{b}{\sqrt3})}
                       {\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt3\,b}{a+\sqrt3\,b}}
 =\frac{a+\sqrt3\,b}{3a+\sqrt3\,b}.
\]

Set this equal to \(\frac{7}{15}\):

\[
\frac{a+\sqrt3\,b}{3a+\sqrt3\,b}= \frac{7}{15}
\Longrightarrow 15(a+\sqrt3\,b)=7(3a+\sqrt3\,b)
\Longrightarrow 6a=8\sqrt3\,b
\Longrightarrow \frac{a}{b}= \frac{4\sqrt3}{3}.
\]

---

### \(\tan B\)

In right \(\triangle ABC\), \(\tan B = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac{AC}{BC}= \dfrac{a}{b}\).

Thus  

\[
\tan B = \frac{4\sqrt3}{3}= \frac{m\sqrt{p}}{n},
\qquad m=4,\; n=3,\; p=3.
\]

Finally  

\[
m+n+p = 4+3+3 = 10.
\]

\[
\boxed{10}
\]

Solution 1:
Let  

\[
C=(0,0),\qquad A=(a,0),\qquad B=(0,b) \qquad (a,b>0)
\]

so that \(\angle C=90^{\circ}\).  
The hypotenuse \(AB\) has equation  

\[
\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1 .
\]

---

### 1.  Locate \(D\) and \(E\)

Since \(CD\) and \(CE\) trisect the right angle, the rays from \(C\) form angles  

\[
\angle ACD = 30^{\circ},\qquad \angle DCE =30^{\circ},\qquad \angle ECB =30^{\circ}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Ray } CD &: (x,y)=t\bigl(\cos30^{\circ},\sin30^{\circ}\bigr)=t\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\tfrac12\Bigr),\\[2mm]
\text{Ray } CE &: (x,y)=s\bigl(\cos60^{\circ},\sin60^{\circ}\bigr)=s\Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

---

#### Point \(D\)

Insert \((x,y)=t(\sqrt3/2,1/2)\) into \(\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1\):

\[
t\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3}{2a}+\frac1{2b}\Bigr)=1\Longrightarrow 
t_{D}= \frac{2ab}{\sqrt3\,b + a } .
\]

Thus  

\[
D=\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3\,ab}{\sqrt3\,b+a},\; \frac{ab}{\sqrt3\,b+a}\Bigr).
\]

#### Point \(E\)

Insert \((x,y)=s(1/2,\sqrt3/2)\):

\[
s\Bigl(\frac1{2a}+\frac{\sqrt3}{2b}\Bigr)=1\Longrightarrow 
s_{E}= \frac{2ab}{b+\sqrt3\,a } .
\]

Thus  

\[
E=\Bigl(\frac{ab}{b+\sqrt3\,a},\; \frac{\sqrt3\,ab}{b+\sqrt3\,a}\Bigr).
\]

---

### 2.  Use a linear parameter on \(AB\)

Points of \(AB\) can be written as  

\[
(x,y)=\bigl(a(1-\lambda),\,b\lambda\bigr),\qquad 0\le\lambda\le1,
\]

where \(\lambda=0\) gives \(A\) and \(\lambda=1\) gives \(B\).

For any point on \(AB\),

\[
\lambda=\frac{y}{b}=1-\frac{x}{a}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\lambda_D=\frac{y_D}{b}= \frac{a}{\sqrt3\,b+a},
\qquad
\lambda_E=\frac{y_E}{b}= \frac{\sqrt3\,a}{b+\sqrt3\,a}.
\]

Because \(D,E,B\) are collinear, the segment ratios are  

\[
\frac{DE}{BE}= \frac{\lambda_E-\lambda_D}{1-\lambda_E}.
\]

Compute:

\[
\frac{DE}{BE}= \frac{\,\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt3 a}{b+\sqrt3 a}-\frac{a}{\sqrt3 b+a}\,}{\,1-\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt3 a}{b+\sqrt3 a}\,}
            =\frac{2a}{a+\sqrt3\,b}.
\]

The problem states \(\displaystyle\frac{DE}{BE}= \frac{8}{15}\); therefore  

\[
\frac{2a}{a+\sqrt3\,b}= \frac{8}{15}
\Longrightarrow 30a = 8a+8\sqrt3\,b
\Longrightarrow 22a = 8\sqrt3\,b
\Longrightarrow \frac{a}{b}= \frac{4\sqrt3}{11}.
\]

---

### 3.  Find \(\tan B\)

At vertex \(B\), the side opposite \(\angle B\) is \(AC = a\) and the side adjacent is \(BC = b\). Hence  

\[
\tan B = \frac{a}{b}= \frac{4\sqrt3}{11}.
\]

Write \(\tan B = \dfrac{m\sqrt{p}}{n}\) with \(m,n\) coprime and \(p\) square‑free:

\[
m=4,\qquad n=11,\qquad p=3.
\]

Thus  

\[
m+n+p = 4+11+3 = 18.
\]

\[
\boxed{18}
\]

<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>You will be given a problem followed by an enumerated list of 4 candidate solutions. Your task is to systematically analyze these solutions to identify the best approach.

Problem: Determine the points at which the function \( f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) defined by
\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 
x & \text{if } x \text{ is irrational} \\ 
p \sin \frac{1}{q} & \text{if } x = \frac{p}{q} \ (\text{rational and irreducible}) 
\end{cases} \]
is continuous.

Solutions:
Solution 0:
**Step 1.  Understand the definition**

\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
x, & x\ \text{irrational},\\[4pt]
p\sin\!\frac{1}{q}, & x=\dfrac{p}{q}\ \text{with }\gcd(p,q)=1 .
\end{cases}
\]

For a rational number \(x=p/q\) we have \(f(x)=p\sin (1/q)\); for an irrational \(x\) we simply have \(f(x)=x\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2.  Continuity at an irrational point \(a\)**  

Let \((x_n)\) be any sequence converging to an irrational \(a\).  

*If \(x_n\) are irrational*, then \(f(x_n)=x_n\to a\).

*If some \(x_n\) are rational*, write \(x_n=p_n/q_n\) (in lowest terms).  
Because the limit is irrational, the denominators must satisfy \(q_n\to\infty\); otherwise we would have only finitely many possible rationals and could not converge to an irrational number.

Now

\[
f(x_n)=p_n\sin\frac{1}{q_n}
      =\frac{p_n}{q_n}\,\bigl(q_n\sin\frac{1}{q_n}\bigr).
\]

Since \(\displaystyle \lim_{q\to\infty}q\sin\frac{1}{q}=1\) (use \(\sin t\sim t\) as \(t\to0\)),
\[
f(x_n)\longrightarrow \frac{p_n}{q_n}=x_n\longrightarrow a .
\]

Thus \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=a=f(a)\).  
**\(f\) is continuous at every irrational number.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3.  Continuity at a rational point \(a=\dfrac{p}{q}\) (in lowest terms)**  

We have \(f(a)=p\sin\frac{1}{q}\).  
Consider a sequence of irrationals \(x_n\to a\); then \(f(x_n)=x_n\to a\).

For continuity we need \(a = p\sin\frac{1}{q}\).  Using \(a=p/q\),

\[
\frac{p}{q}=p\sin\frac{1}{q}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{1}{q}= \sin\frac{1}{q}.
\]

The equation \(\sin t = t\) has only the solution \(t=0\) (for \(t>0\), \(\sin t < t\)).  
Hence we would need \(\frac{1}{q}=0\), which is impossible for a finite integer \(q\).

The only remaining possibility is \(p=0\), i.e. the rational number \(0\).  
Indeed, for \(a=0\) we have \(f(0)=0\), and for any sequence \(x_n\to 0\),

* if \(x_n\) are irrational, \(f(x_n)=x_n\to0\);
* if \(x_n=p_n/q_n\) are rational, \(|f(x_n)| = |p_n\sin(1/q_n)|\le |p_n|\to0\) because \(p_n/q_n\to0\).

Thus \(f\) is continuous at \(0\).

For any non‑zero rational \(a\) we have a mismatch between the limit along irrationals (\(a\)) and the value \(f(a)=p\sin(1/q)\neq a\). Hence \(f\) is **discontinuous at every non‑zero rational**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4.  Collect the continuity points**

\[
\text{Continuous at } \; 0 \;\; \text{and at every irrational number.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[
\boxed{\; \{0\}\ \cup\ \bigl(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}\bigr)\;}
\]

So \(f\) is continuous exactly at \(0\) and at all irrational points, and it is discontinuous at every non‑zero rational.

Solution 1:
For a real number \(x\) write  

\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
x , & x\notin\mathbb{Q},\\[2mm]
p\sin \dfrac{1}{q}, & x=\dfrac{p}{q}\;(p,q\in\mathbb Z,\;q>0,\;\gcd(p,q)=1).
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 1.  Continuity at a rational point  

Let \(a=\dfrac{p_{0}}{q_{0}}\) be rational (in lowest terms).  
If \(x\to a\) through irrational numbers, then \(f(x)=x\) and  

\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to a\\ x\notin\mathbb Q}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a}x = a .
\]

Hence, for \(f\) to be continuous at \(a\) we would need  

\[
f(a)=a .
\]

But  

\[
f(a)=p_{0}\sin\frac{1}{q_{0}},\qquad a=\frac{p_{0}}{q_{0}} .
\]

Thus continuity would require  

\[
p_{0}\sin\frac{1}{q_{0}} = \frac{p_{0}}{q_{0}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sin\frac{1}{q_{0}}=\frac{1}{q_{0}} .
\]

The equation \(\sin t = t\) has the unique solution \(t=0\).  
Since \(t=\frac{1}{q_{0}}>0\), the equality cannot hold. Consequently  

\[
f(a)\neq a,
\]

so the limit of \(f\) at a rational point is different from the value of \(f\) there.  
\[
\boxed{\text{The function is discontinuous at every rational point.}}
\]

---

### 2.  Continuity at an irrational point  

Let \(\xi\) be irrational. We must show that  

\[
\lim_{x\to \xi} f(x)=\xi .
\]

Take any \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\in\mathbb N\) so large that  

\[
\frac{1}{N^{2}}<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Because \(\xi\) is irrational, there exists a \(\delta>0\) such that **every** rational number
\(\dfrac{p}{q}\) satisfying \(\bigl| \dfrac{p}{q}-\xi\bigr|<\delta\) has denominator \(q\ge N\)
(this is a standard consequence of the fact that rationals with bounded denominator form a
discrete set).

Now let \(x\) with \(|x-\xi|<\delta\).

*If \(x\) is irrational*, then \(f(x)=x\) and  

\[
|f(x)-\xi| = |x-\xi| < \varepsilon .
\]

*If \(x=\dfrac{p}{q}\) is rational*, then \(q\ge N\) and  

\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x)-\xi|
&= \Bigl|p\sin\frac{1}{q}-\xi\Bigr| \\
&\le \Bigl|p\sin\frac{1}{q}-\frac{p}{q}\Bigr|
      +\Bigl|\frac{p}{q}-\xi\Bigr| .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(|p/q-\xi|<\delta<\varepsilon/2\), it remains to estimate the first term.
Using the Taylor expansion \(\sin t = t-\frac{t^{3}}{6}+O(t^{5})\),

\[
\Bigl|\sin\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q}\Bigr|
= \frac{1}{6q^{3}}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{q^{5}}\right)
\le \frac{1}{5q^{3}}\quad (q\ge 1).
\]

Hence  

\[
\Bigl|p\sin\frac{1}{q}-\frac{p}{q}\Bigr|
= |p|\,\Bigl|\sin\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{q}\Bigr|
\le |p|\frac{1}{5q^{3}}
= \frac{|p|}{q}\,\frac{1}{5q^{2}}
\le (|\xi|+1)\frac{1}{5N^{2}}
<\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
\]

for \(N\) chosen as above. Consequently  

\[
|f(x)-\xi|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}=\varepsilon .
\]

Thus for every \(\varepsilon>0\) a \(\delta>0\) exists such that \(|x-\xi|<\delta\) implies
\(|f(x)-\xi|<\varepsilon\); i.e.  

\[
\boxed{\text{\(f\) is continuous at every irrational point.}}
\]

---

### 3.  Set of continuity points  

Combining the two parts we obtain  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\text{The function }f\text{ is continuous exactly at the irrational numbers, and discontinuous at all rational numbers.}}
\]

Solution 2:
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
x, & x\notin\mathbb Q,\\[4pt]
p\sin\frac1q, & x=\dfrac pq\ \text{with }p,q\in\mathbb Z,\;q>0,\;\gcd(p,q)=1 .
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 1.  Behaviour near an irrational point  

Let \(a\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\).  
Take any sequence \(x_n\to a\).

*If \(x_n\) are irrational*, then \(f(x_n)=x_n\to a\).

*If \(x_n=\dfrac{p_n}{q_n}\) are rational*, then  

\[
\bigl|f(x_n)-x_n\bigr|
   =\Bigl|p_n\sin\frac1{q_n}-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\Bigr|
   =|p_n|\,\Bigl|\sin\frac1{q_n}-\frac1{q_n}\Bigr|.
\]

Since \(p_n = x_n q_n\),

\[
|f(x_n)-x_n| = |x_n|\,q_n\Bigl|\sin\frac1{q_n}-\frac1{q_n}\Bigr|.
\]

For large \(q\) we have the Taylor estimate  

\[
\Bigl|\sin\frac1q-\frac1q\Bigr|\le \frac{C}{q^{3}}
\qquad (C>0\text{ constant}),
\]

so  

\[
|f(x_n)-x_n| \le |x_n|\,\frac{C}{q_n^{2}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0 .
\]

Thus \(f(x_n)\to a\) for every sequence \(x_n\to a\); therefore  

\[
\boxed{\;f\text{ is continuous at every irrational point. }\;}
\]

---

### 2.  Behaviour at a rational point  

Let \(a=\dfrac{p_0}{q_0}\) (in lowest terms). Then  

\[
f(a)=p_0\sin\frac1{q_0}.
\]

Approach \(a\) with irrational numbers \(x\to a\).  
For such \(x\), \(f(x)=x\to a=\dfrac{p_0}{q_0}\).

Hence the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\to a\) (through irrationals) equals \(\dfrac{p_0}{q_0}\), which coincides with \(f(a)\) **iff**

\[
p_0\sin\frac1{q_0}= \frac{p_0}{q_0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sin\frac1{q_0}= \frac1{q_0}.
\]

The equation \(\sin t = t\) has the unique real solution \(t=0\); but \(\frac1{q_0}>0\) for any finite \(q_0\). Therefore the equality never holds for a genuine rational number.

Consequently the one‑sided limit (through irrationals) differs from the value \(f(a)\); the function is **discontinuous at every rational point**.

---

### 3.  Summary  

\[
\boxed{\; f \text{ is continuous precisely at the irrational real numbers, and discontinuous at every rational number. }\;}
\]

Solution 3:
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
x , & x\notin \mathbb Q,\\[2mm]
p\sin\!\dfrac1q , & x=\dfrac pq\;(p,q\in\mathbb Z,\;q>0,\;\gcd (p,q)=1).
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 1.  Behaviour of \(f\) on rationals with large denominator  

If \(x=\dfrac pq\) and \(q\) is large, then  

\[
\sin\!\frac1q = \frac1q+O\!\left(\frac1{q^{3}}\right) ,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
f\!\left(\frac pq\right)=p\sin\!\frac1q
        =\frac pq+O\!\left(\frac{p}{q^{3}}\right)
        =x+O\!\left(\frac1{q^{2}}\right).
\]

Hence for rationals whose denominator \(q\) is large, \(f(x)\) is arbitrarily close
to the rational number itself.

---

### 2.  Limit of \(f(x)\) at an arbitrary point \(a\)

Let \(a\in\mathbb R\) and let \(\varepsilon>0\) be given.

*Choose \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that \(\dfrac{2}{N}<\varepsilon\).*

Only finitely many reduced fractions \(\dfrac pq\) satisfy \(|q|\le N\); call this
finite set \(S\).
Since these points are isolated, we can choose \(\delta_1>0\) so small that

\[
(a-\delta_1,\;a+\delta_1)\cap S=\begin{cases}
\{a\},& a\in S,\\[1mm]
\varnothing ,& a\notin S .
\end{cases}
\]

Now let  

\[
\delta=\min\!\bigl(\delta_1,\; \tfrac{1}{N}\bigr).
\]

If \(|x-a|<\delta\) we have two possibilities.

1. **\(x\) irrational.**  
   Then \(f(x)=x\) and \(|f(x)-a|=|x-a|<\varepsilon\).

2. **\(x=\dfrac pq\) rational.**  

   * If \(|q|\le N\) then, by the choice of \(\delta\), the only such rational
     in the interval is possibly \(x=a\) itself; in that case
     \(|f(x)-a|=|f(a)-a|\) will be dealt with separately below.

   * If \(|q|> N\) then, using the estimate from step 1,
     \[
     |f(x)-x|=|p\sin\!\tfrac1q-\tfrac pq|
            \le \frac{C}{q^{2}}\le \frac{C}{N^{2}}
            <\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
     \]
     and therefore
     \[
     |f(x)-a|\le |f(x)-x|+|x-a|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
                =\varepsilon .
     \]

Thus for every \(a\) we have  

\[
\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=a .
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 3.  Where does the function equal its limit?

From (1) the only possible points of continuity are those where
\(f(a)=a\).

*If \(a\) is irrational*: \(f(a)=a\) by definition, so every irrational
point is a continuity point.

*If \(a\) is rational*, write \(a=\dfrac pq\) in lowest terms.  
Then \(f(a)=p\sin\!\dfrac1q\). Equality \(f(a)=a\) would require  

\[
p\sin\!\frac1q=\frac pq\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sin\!\frac1q=\frac1q .
\]

The equation \(\sin t=t\) has the unique solution \(t=0\); hence
\(\frac1q=0\), which is impossible for a finite integer \(q\).
Consequently \(f(a)=a\) can hold only when \(p=0\), i.e. at \(a=0\).

At \(a=0\) we have \(f(0)=0\cdot\sin 1=0\), and by (1) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=0\);
thus \(f\) is continuous at \(0\).

For any other rational \(a\neq0\) we have \(f(a)\neq a\) while the limit is \(a\);
hence \(f\) is discontinuous there.

---

### 4.  Set of continuity points

\[
\boxed{\; \text{The function }f \text{ is continuous at every irrational }x
\text{ and at }x=0,\;
\text{and discontinuous at all other rational points.}\;}
\]

The Shannon entropy of the discrete output is \[ \begin{aligned} H_k &=-\sum_{s=0}^{2^{k}-2}\frac12\,2^{-s}\log_2\!\Big(\frac12\,2^{-s}\Big) -2^{-\,(2^{k}-1)}\log_2\!\big(2^{-\,(2^{k}-1)}\big) \\[4pt] &=\frac12\sum_{s=0}^{N-1}(1+s)2^{-s}+N\,2^{-N}, \qquad N=2^{k}-1 . \end{aligned} \] The two finite sums have a closed‑form expression \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{s=0}^{N-1}2^{-s}&=2\bigl(1-2^{-N}\bigr),\\[4pt] \sum_{s=0}^{N-1}s2^{-s}&= \frac{\tfrac12-N\,2^{-N}+(N-1)2^{-(N+1)}}{(1-\tfrac12)^2} =2- (N+2)2^{-N}. \end{aligned} \] Substituting gives \[ \boxed{H_k=2\bigl(1-2^{-N}\bigr)-\tfrac12 (N+2)2^{-N}+N2^{-N}} \;=\;2-\bigl(1+N\bigr)2^{-N}, \qquad N=2^{k}-1. \] Hence \[ H_k = 2-\bigl(1+2^{k}-1\bigr)2^{-(2^{k}-1)} = 2-\bigl(2^{k}\bigr)2^{-(2^{k}-1)} . \] Because \(2^{k}2^{-(2^{k}-1)}\) decays **super‑exponentially** with \(k\), the second term becomes negligible already for modest \(k\). --- **2.
